module control_register_block (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input enable,
  input [n-1:0] data_in,
  input [m-1:0] control,
  output [n-1:0] out
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits in the data input and output signals
parameter m = 4; // number of bits in the control signal

reg [n-1:0] data_reg; // register to store the input data
reg [n-1:0] default_data = 0; // default value for the data register

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) begin
    data_reg <= default_data; // reset the data register
  end else if (enable) begin
    data_reg <= data_in; // store the input data
  end
end

always @(*) begin
  case (control)
    // define the control pattern to output the stored data
    4'b0001: out = data_reg;
    4'b0010: out = data_reg;
    4'b0100: out = data_reg;
    4'b1000: out = data_reg;
    default: out = 0; // default output value
  endcase
end

endmodule

module binary_counter(

    input rst,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

end

A round and saturation block is a type of digital circuit that can be used to round a number to the nearest integer and to prevent overflow and underflow.

Outputs: a signed fixed-point number (out)

The module should implement the following functionality:

The input number (in) should be rounded to the nearest integer, using standard rounding rules.
If the rounded number is too large to be represented in the output format, the output should be the maximum representable value (i.e., saturation).
If the rounded number is too small to be represented in the output format, the output should be the minimum representable value (i.e., saturation).
The output number (out) should have the same number of integer bits (ib) and fractional bits (fb) as the input number.
To implement the round and saturation block, you should use Verilog code to perform the rounding and to check for overflow and underflow. 
You should then use these calculations to connect the input to the output.
Finally, you should use the output to represent the result of the round and saturation block.

module round_saturation (
  input signed [ib+fb-1:0] in,
  output signed [ib+fb-1:0] out
);

parameter ib = 4; // number of integer bits
parameter fb = 8; // number of fractional bits

integer round_val;
integer max_val;
integer min_val;
integer in_val;

assign in_val = in * (2 ** fb); // Shift input to left by fb bits to convert to integer

always @(*) begin
  if (in_val >= 0) begin
    round_val = (in_val + (2 ** (fb - 1))) >> fb; // Round up if fractional part is greater than or equal to 0.5
  end else begin
    round_val = (in_val - (2 ** (fb - 1))) >> fb; // Round down if fractional part is less than 0.5
  end
  
  max_val = (2 ** (ib + fb - 1)) - 1; // Calculate maximum representable value
  min_val = -(2 ** (ib + fb - 1)); // Calculate minimum representable value
  
  if (round_val > max_val) begin
    out = max_val; // Saturation: Output maximum representable value if rounded value is too large
  end else if (round_val < min_val) begin
    out = min_val; // Saturation: Output minimum representable value if rounded value is too small
  end else begin
    out = round_val; // Output rounded value
  end
end

endmodule

);

module shift_register (

    input load,
    input serial_in,
    output reg [2:0] out
);

module binary_counter (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input enable,
  output reg [3:0] count
);

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
      count <= 4'b0000;
    end else if (enable) begin
      count <= count + 1;
    end
  end

endmodule

  input clk,
  input reset,
  input direction,
  output reg [3:0] count
);

  if (reset) begin
    count <= 4'b0000;
  end else if (direction) begin
    if (count == 4'b1111) begin
      count <= 4'b0000;
    end else begin
      count <= count + 1;

  end
end

module single_port_ram (
  input wire clk,
  input wire en,
  input wire we,
  input wire [10:0] addr,
  input wire [7:0] din,
  output wire [7:0] dout
);

      else begin

The duration of the output pulse is determined by the values of two external resistors and a capacitor.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a trigger signal (trig), a reset signal (rst)
Outputs: a single output pulse (out)

Your module should also have the following parameters:

w: the width of the output pulse in clock cycles
r1: the resistance of the first external resistor
r2: the resistance of the second external resistor
c: the capacitance of the capacitor

Your module should implement the following functionality:

When the trigger signal goes high, the circuit should produce a single output pulse with a duration of w clock cycles.
The output pulse should be synchronized with the clock signal.
The reset signal should immediately terminate any output pulse that is currently being generated.
The duration of the output pulse should be determined by the values of the external resistors and capacitor, according to the following formula:

t = 0.69 * (r1 + r2) * c

where t is the duration of the output pulse in seconds.

To implement the one-shot pulse generator, you should use Verilog code to define the timing and pulse-width calculation based on the input signals and parameters. 
You should also use the clock signal to synchronize the output pulse with the system clock. 
Finally, you should use the reset signal to immediately terminate any output pulse that is currently being generated.
Response:
module one_shot_pulse_generator (
  input trig, // trigger signal
  input rst, // reset signal
  input clk, // system clock
  output reg out // output pulse
);

parameter w = 10; // width of the output pulse in clock cycles
parameter r1 = 1000; // resistance of the first external resistor
parameter r2 = 1000; // resistance of the second external resistor
parameter c = 1e-6; // capacitance of the capacitor

reg [31:0] count; // counter for pulse width
real t; // duration of the output pulse in seconds

always @(*) begin
  t = 0.69 * (r1 + r2) * c; // calculate pulse duration
end

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin
    out <= 0; // reset output pulse
    count <= 0; // reset pulse width counter
  end else if (trig) begin
    out <= 1; // start output pulse
    count <= 0; // reset pulse width counter
  end else if (out) begin
    count <= count + 1; // increment pulse width counter
    if (count >= w) begin
      out <= 0; // end output pulse
    end
  end
end

endmodule

module flip_flop (
    input wire D,
    input wire DE,
    input wire VPWR,
    input wire VGND,
    input wire VPB,
    input wire VNB,
    input wire CLK,
    output reg Q,
    output reg Q_N
);

    // Asynchronous reset
    always @ (VGND or VPWR)
    begin
        if (VGND == 0 || VPWR == 1) begin
            Q <= 0;
            Q_N <= 1;
        end
    end

    // Positive edge-triggered flip-flop
    always @ (posedge CLK)
    begin
        if (DE == 1) begin
            Q <= D;
            Q_N <= ~D;
        end
    end

endmodule

);

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a stepper motor controller. 
A stepper motor is a type of motor that moves in small, precise steps. 
To control a stepper motor, you need to sequence the current through each of its coils in a specific pattern. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a step signal (step), a direction signal (dir), and a clock signal (clk)
Outputs: four signals (coil1, coil2, coil3, coil4) that control the current through the four coils of the stepper motor
The module should also have the following parameters:

steps_per_rev: the number of steps required to complete one revolution of the stepper motor
Your module should implement the following functionality:

The circuit should have four output signals, one for each of the coils of the stepper motor.
The circuit should sequence the current through the coils in a specific pattern to move the stepper motor in the desired direction and number of steps.
The circuit should use pulse width modulation (PWM) to control the speed of the stepper motor.
To implement the stepper motor controller, you should use Verilog code to define the sequence of current through the coils. 
You should then use this sequence to control the output signals (coil1, coil2, coil3, coil4) based on the step and direction inputs. 
You should also use PWM to control the speed of the stepper motor by adjusting the duty cycle of the output signals.
Response:
module stepper_motor_controller (
  input step,
  input dir,
  input clk,
  output coil1,
  output coil2,
  output coil3,
  output coil4
);

parameter steps_per_rev = 200; // number of steps per revolution

reg [1:0] state = 2'b00; // current state of the stepper motor
reg [7:0] counter = 8'd0; // counter for PWM

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (step) begin
    if (dir) begin
      // clockwise rotation
      case (state)
        2'b00: begin coil1 <= 1; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b01; end
        2'b01: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 1; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b11; end
        2'b11: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 1; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b10; end
        2'b10: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 1; state <= 2'b00; end
      endcase
    end else begin
      // counter-clockwise rotation
      case (state)
        2'b00: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 1; state <= 2'b10; end
        2'b10: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 1; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b11; end
        2'b11: begin coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 1; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b01; end
        2'b01: begin coil1 <= 1; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 0; state <= 2'b00; end
      endcase
    end
    counter <= counter + 1;
    if (counter >= steps_per_rev) begin
      counter <= 0;
    end
  end else begin
    coil1 <= 0; coil2 <= 0; coil3 <= 0; coil4 <= 0;
  end
end

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (counter < steps_per_rev/2) begin
    coil1 <= 0;
    coil2 <= 0;
    coil3 <= 0;
    coil4 <= 0;
  end else begin
    case (state)
      2'b00: coil1 <= 1;
      2'b01: coil2 <= 1;
      2'b11: coil3 <= 1;
      2'b10: coil4 <= 1;
    endcase
  end
end

endmodule

  d. If the two least significant bits of `Q` are `11` or `00`, do nothing.
  e. Shift `A` and `Q` to the right by 1 bit.
  f. Set the most significant bit of `Q` to the sign bit of `A`.

);

module phy_clock_io #
  (
   parameter TCQ          = 100,       // clk->out delay (sim only)
   parameter CK_WIDTH     = 2,         // # of clock output pairs
   parameter WRLVL        = "OFF",     // Enable write leveling
   parameter DRAM_TYPE    = "DDR3",    // Memory I/F type: "DDR3", "DDR2"
   parameter REFCLK_FREQ  = 300.0,     // IODELAY Reference Clock freq (MHz)
   parameter IODELAY_GRP  = "IODELAY_MIG"  // May be assigned unique name
                                              // when mult IP cores in design
   )
  (
   input                 clk_mem,   // full rate core clock
   input                 clk,       // half rate core clock
   input                 rst,       // half rate core clk reset
   output [CK_WIDTH-1:0] ddr_ck_p,  // forwarded diff. clock to memory
   output [CK_WIDTH-1:0] ddr_ck_n   // forwarded diff. clock to memory
   );

  //***************************************************************************

  generate
    genvar ck_i;
    for (ck_i = 0; ck_i < CK_WIDTH; ck_i = ck_i + 1) begin: gen_ck
      phy_ck_iob #
        (
         .TCQ            (TCQ),
         .WRLVL          (WRLVL),
         .DRAM_TYPE      (DRAM_TYPE),
         .REFCLK_FREQ    (REFCLK_FREQ),
         .IODELAY_GRP    (IODELAY_GRP)
         )
        u_phy_ck_iob
          (
           .clk_mem   (clk_mem),
           .clk       (clk),
           .rst       (rst),
           .ddr_ck_p  (ddr_ck_p[ck_i]),
           .ddr_ck_n  (ddr_ck_n[ck_i])
           );
    end
  endgenerate

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a memory management unit (MMU). 
An MMU is a hardware component that maps virtual addresses to physical addresses in a computer system. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- a virtual address (va) of width w
- a page table (pt) of size 2^w
- a page table base address (pba) of width w

Outputs: 
- a physical address (pa) of width w
- a valid signal (valid) indicating whether the physical address is valid

Your module should implement the following functionality:

The virtual address should be used to index into the page table.
The page table entry at the indexed location should contain the physical page number.
The physical page number should be concatenated with the page offset of the virtual address to form the physical address.
If the page table entry is invalid, the valid signal should be set to 0.

To implement the MMU, you should use Verilog code to define the page table as an array of physical page numbers. 
You should then use the virtual address to index into the page table and retrieve the physical page number.
Finally, you should concatenate the physical page number with the page offset of the virtual address to form the physical address and set the valid signal based on the validity of the page table entry.

module MMU (
  input [w-1:0] va,
  input [2**w-1:0] pt,
  input [w-1:0] pba,
  output [w-1:0] pa,
  output valid
);

parameter w = 8; // width of virtual and physical addresses

reg [w-1:0] vpn; // virtual page number
reg [w-1:0] pfn; // physical frame number
reg [w-1:0] offset; // page offset
reg [w-1:0] pte; // page table entry

assign vpn = va[w-1:w-1-log2(w)]; // extract virtual page number
assign offset = va[w-1-log2(w)-1:0]; // extract page offset

always @(*) begin
  pte = pt[vpn]; // retrieve page table entry
  if (pte == 0) begin
    valid = 0; // invalid page table entry
  end else begin
    valid = 1; // valid page table entry
    pfn = pte; // retrieve physical frame number
    pa = {pfn, offset}; // concatenate physical frame number and page offset
  end
end

endmodule

  input load,
  input [15:0] load_val,

);

The counter output should be displayed on a 4-bit output port.

module synchronous_counter(
    input clk, // clock input
    input reset, // reset input
    output reg [3:0] count // 4-bit output port
);

always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
    if (reset) begin
        count <= 4'b0000; // reset count to 0
    end else begin
        if (count == 4'b1001) begin
            count <= 4'b0000; // reset count to 0 when it reaches 9
        end else begin
            count <= count + 1; // increment count by 1
        end
    end
end

endmodule

You are tasked with designing a Verilog module that implements the Clarke Transform. The Clarke Transform is used to convert balanced three-phase quantities into balanced two-phase quantities. The A and B phases are converted to the direct axis (alpha) component and the quadrature axis (beta) component. The alpha and beta components are still dependent on time and speed. Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:
- `phase_currents_0`: a signed 18-bit fixed-point number representing the current in phase A.
- `phase_currents_1`: a signed 18-bit fixed-point number representing the current in phase B.

- `alpha_current`: a signed 18-bit fixed-point number representing the direct axis (alpha) component.
- `beta_current`: a signed 18-bit fixed-point number representing the quadrature axis (beta) component.

Your module should implement the following equations:

```
alpha_current = 2/3 * phase_currents_0 - 1/3 * phase_currents_1
beta_current = 1/sqrt(3) * phase_currents_1
               + 1/sqrt(3) * phase_currents_0 
               - 1/sqrt(3) * phase_currents_2
```

You should assume that the input signals are sampled at a constant rate, and that the calculations should be performed for each sample.

Your module should be implemented within 200 lines of Verilog code.

    input signed [17:0] phase_currents_0,
    input signed [17:0] phase_currents_1,
    output signed [17:0] alpha_current,
    output signed [17:0] beta_current
);

    wire signed [17:0] sqrt3 = 18102; // sqrt(3) in sfix18_En15 format

    assign alpha_current = (2 * phase_currents_0 - phase_currents_1) * 10923; // 2/3 in sfix18_En15 format
    assign beta_current = (phase_currents_1 + phase_currents_0 - (phase_currents_2 << 1)) * 6055; // 1/sqrt(3) in sfix18_En15 format

endmodule

The module should be able to write data to the specified address when the write enable input is high and read data from the specified address when the write enable input is low. Design a Verilog module `memory` that implements the above functionality. The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

- `clk`: clock input
- `wEnb`: write enable input
- `addr`: address input
- `wData`: write data input
- `rData`: read data output

The module should have the following parameters:

- `MEMD`: memory depth
- `DATAW`: data width
- `IZERO`: binary, indicating whether to initialize memory with zeros or not
- `IFILE`: optional hex file to initialize memory from, without the extension.

You can assume that the inputs and outputs are valid and that the address input will not exceed the memory depth.

module memory
 #( parameter MEMD   = 512, // memory depth
    parameter DATAW  = 32 , // data width
    parameter IZERO  = 0  , // binary / Initial RAM with zeros (has priority over IFILE)
    parameter IFILE  = "" ) // initialization hex file (don't pass extension), optional
  ( input                    clk  ,  // clock
    input                    wEnb ,  // write enable for port B
    input  [`log2(MEMD)-1:0] addr ,  // write/read address
    input  [DATAW      -1:0] wData,  // write data
    output reg [DATAW  -1:0] rData); // read  data

  // initialize RAM, with zeros if IZERO or file if IFLE.
  integer i;
  reg [DATAW-1:0] mem [0:MEMD-1]; // memory array
  initial
    if (IZERO)
      for (i=0; i<MEMD; i=i+1) mem[i] = {DATAW{1'b0}};
    else
      if (IFILE != "") $readmemh({IFILE,".hex"}, mem);

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    // write/read; nonblocking statement to read old data
    if (wEnb) begin
      mem[addr] <= wData; // Change into blocking statement (=) to read new data
      rData     <= wData; // flow-through
    end else
      rData <= mem[addr]; //Change into blocking statement (=) to read new data
  end

endmodule

You are tasked with designing a counter module that can increment or decrement based on the input signal, with the ability to load a specific value and auto-wrap around when the maximum or minimum value is reached. The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:
- `clk`: clock signal
- `in`: amount to increment or decrement the counter by
- `en`: enable signal
- `dir`: direction signal (0 for increment, 1 for decrement)
- `autowrap`: auto-wrap signal (1 for enabled, 0 for disabled)
- `load`: load signal (1 for enabled, 0 for disabled)
- `load_data`: data to load into the counter when `load` is enabled

Outputs:
- `count`: current count value
- `wraparound`: wraparound signal (1 for wraparound, 0 for no wraparound)

The counter should be able to handle any width of data inputs.

Design a counter module that meets the above requirements and provide a testbench to verify its functionality.
Response:
module counter #(parameter DW = 32)
(
    input clk,
    input in,
    input en,
    input dir,
    input autowrap,
    input load,
    input [DW-1:0] load_data,
    output reg [DW-1:0] count,
    output reg wraparound
);

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (load) begin
            count <= load_data;
        end else if (en) begin
            if (dir) begin
                count <= count - in;
            end else begin
                count <= count + in;
            end
            if (autowrap) begin
                if (dir) begin
                    if (count == 0) begin
                        count <= {(DW){1'b1}};
                        wraparound <= 1;
                    end
                end else begin
                    if (count == {(DW){1'b1}}) begin
                        count <= 0;
                        wraparound <= 1;
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

endmodule

wire [ABUSWIDTH-1:0] IP_ADD;
wire [7:0] IP_DATA_IN;
wire [7:0] IP_DATA_OUT;

- `sload`: a synchronous load input. When high, the counter should be loaded with the value from the `data` input.

module counter (

  input clock,
  input clk_en,
  input cnt_en,
  input aset,
  input sload,

);

Implement the module `counter` with the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:
- `clk` (1-bit): clock signal
- `rst` (1-bit): asynchronous reset signal
- `en` (1-bit): enable signal
- `load` (1-bit): load signal
- `data_in` (32-bit): new value to be loaded into the counter when `load` is asserted

Outputs:
- `count` (32-bit): current count value of the counter

The module should have the following behavior:
- When `rst` is asserted, the counter should be reset to 0.
- When `en` is asserted, the counter should count up on every positive edge of `clk`.
- When `en` is deasserted, the counter should stop counting.
- When `load` is asserted, the counter should be loaded with the value of `data_in`.
Response:
module counter (
    input clk,
    input rst,
    input en,
    input load,
    input [31:0] data_in,
    output reg [31:0] count
);

always @(posedge clk or negedge rst) begin
    if (!rst) begin
        count <= 0;
    end else if (load) begin
        count <= data_in;
    end else if (en) begin
        count <= count + 1;
    end
end

endmodule

module xor_gate (
    input A,
    input B,
    input EN,
    input CLK,
    output reg Z
);

    always @(posedge CLK) begin
        if (EN) begin
            Z <= A ^ B;
        end else begin
            Z <= 0;
        end
    end

endmodule

- `reset`: the reset signal

- `data_in`: the data to be loaded into the shift register when the `load` signal is high.
- `shift_en`: the shift enable signal - when this signal is high, the shift register should shift the data in the register.
- `shift_left`: the shift direction signal - when this signal is high, the shift register should shift the data to the left. Otherwise, it should shift to the right.

Outputs:
- `data_out`: the data output from the shift register.

The shift register should be 16 bits wide.

module shift_register(
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input load,
    input [15:0] data_in,
    input shift_en,
    input shift_left,
    output reg [15:0] data_out
);

always @(posedge clk, posedge reset) begin
    if (reset) begin
        data_out <= 16'b0;
    end else if (load) begin
        data_out <= data_in;
    end else if (shift_en) begin
        if (shift_left) begin
            data_out <= {data_out[14:0], 1'b0};
        end else begin
            data_out <= {1'b0, data_out[15:1]};
        end
    end
end

endmodule

Your task is to complete the CLOCK module by filling in the missing parts of the code.

The CLOCK module has four input and output ports:

- CLK32: a 32.000MHz input clock signal
- PixelClk: the 41.600MHz output clock signal
- PixelClk2: the 83.200MHz output clock signal
- PixelClk10: the 416.000MHz output clock signal
- SerDesStrobe: the 832.000MHz output clock signal

The CLOCK module includes a PLL module called ClockGenPLL, which generates three clock signals with frequencies of 416.000MHz, 83.200MHz, and 41.600MHz. The PLL module has several input and output ports, including the following:

- CLKIN: the input clock signal (CLK32)
- CLKFBIN: the feedback clock signal (pll_fbout)
- CLKOUT0: the output clock signal with the lowest frequency (pll_clk10x)
- CLKOUT1: the intermediate output clock signal (pll_clk2x)
- CLKOUT2: the output clock signal with the highest frequency (pll_clk1x)
- LOCKED: a signal that indicates whether the PLL is locked to the input clock signal (pll_locked)

The CLOCK module includes two BUFG (Buffered Global) modules, which buffer the pll_clk1x and pll_clk2x signals to generate the PixelClk and PixelClk2 output clock signals, respectively. The CLOCK module also includes a BUFPLL (Buffered PLL) module, which buffers the pll_clk10x signal to generate the PixelClk10 and SerDesStrobe output clock signals.

You need to fill in the missing parts of the CLOCK module to generate the four output clock signals.

module CLOCK
( input CLK32,
  output PixelClk,
  output PixelClk2,
  output PixelClk10,
  output SerDesStrobe
);

  wire pll_fbout;      // PLL Feedback
  wire pll_clk10x;     // From PLL to BUFPLL
  wire pll_clk2x;      // From PLL to BUFG
  wire pll_clk1x;      // From PLL to BUFG
  wire pll_locked;

  PLL_BASE #(.CLKOUT0_DIVIDE(2),   // IO clock 416.000MHz (VCO / 2)
             .CLKOUT1_DIVIDE(10),  // Intermediate clock 83.200MHz (VCO / 10)
             .CLKOUT2_DIVIDE(20),  // Pixel Clock 41.600MHz (VCO / 20)
             .CLKFBOUT_MULT(26),   // VCO = 32.000MHz * 26 = 832.000MHz ...
             .DIVCLK_DIVIDE(1),    // ... 832.000MHz / 1 = 832.000MHz
             .CLKIN_PERIOD(31.25)  // 31.25ns = 32.000MHz
            ) ClockGenPLL(.CLKIN(CLK32),
                          .CLKFBIN(pll_fbout),
                          .RST(1'b0),
                          .CLKOUT0(pll_clk10x),
                          .CLKOUT1(pll_clk2x),
                          .CLKOUT2(pll_clk1x),
                          .CLKOUT3(),
                          .CLKOUT4(),
                          .CLKOUT5(),
                          .CLKFBOUT(pll_fbout),
                          .LOCKED(pll_locked));

  BUFG Clk1x_buf(.I(pll_clk1x), .O(PixelClk));
  BUFG Clk2x_buf(.I(pll_clk2x), .O(PixelClk2));
  
  BUFPLL #(.DIVIDE(5),
           .ENABLE_SYNC("TRUE")
          ) Clk10x_buf(.PLLIN(pll_clk10x),
                       .GCLK(PixelClk2),
                       .LOCKED(pll_locked),
                       .IOCLK(PixelClk10),
                       .SERDESSTROBE(SerDesStrobe),
                       .LOCK());

endmodule

Reed-Solomon codes are used for error correction in data transmission and storage systems. 
The encoder takes a message of k symbols and adds redundancy to produce a codeword of n symbols. 
The decoder takes a received codeword of n symbols, and uses the redundancy to correct up to t errors in the received symbols.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

- t: the number of errors that can be corrected

- [n-1:0] received: the received codeword to be decoded (or the encoded codeword to be transmitted)

Outputs:
- [n-1:0] encoded: the encoded codeword
- [k-1:0] decoded: the decoded message

Your module should implement the following functionality:

Encoder:
- Generate a generator polynomial of degree n-k with roots at α^(n-k+i), i=0,1,...,k-1, where α is a primitive element of a finite field GF(2^m)
- Use the generator polynomial to encode the message
- The encoded message should be the polynomial remainder when the message polynomial is divided by the generator polynomial
- Append the remainder to the message to produce the codeword

Decoder:
- Generate a syndrome polynomial by evaluating the received polynomial at α^i, i=1,2,...,2t
- Use the syndrome polynomial to find the locations of the errors in the received polynomial
- Use the error locations to determine the error values
- Correct the errors in the received polynomial to produce the message polynomial
- Extract the message from the message polynomial

To implement the Reed-Solomon encoder and decoder, you should use Verilog code to define the polynomial operations as functions of the input symbols. 
You should then use these functions to implement the encoder and decoder.

The light should stay green for 10 seconds, then switch to yellow for 2 seconds, and finally switch to red for 8 seconds. After the red light has been on for 8 seconds, the light should switch back to green and the cycle should repeat indefinitely.

Design a Verilog module that controls the traffic light and outputs the current state of the light as a 3-bit signal, where 2'b00 represents green, 2'b01 represents yellow, and 2'b10 represents red. The module should have a single input, 'clk', which is a 50 MHz clock signal, and a single output, 'state', which is the 3-bit signal representing the current state of the traffic light.

Assume that the initial state of the traffic light is green.

module traffic_light(clk, state);
    input clk;
    output reg [2:0] state;

    reg [31:0] counter;

    always @(posedge clk)
    begin
        counter <= counter + 1;

        case(state)
            3'b000: // Green state
                begin
                    if(counter >= 10_000_000) // 10 seconds
                    begin
                        counter <= 0;
                        state <= 3'b001; // Switch to yellow
                    end
                end

            3'b001: // Yellow state
                begin
                    if(counter >= 2_000_000) // 2 seconds
                    begin
                        counter <= 0;
                        state <= 3'b010; // Switch to red
                    end
                end

            3'b010: // Red state
                begin
                    if(counter >= 8_000_000) // 8 seconds
                    begin
                        counter <= 0;
                        state <= 3'b000; // Switch to green
                    end
                end
        endcase
    end
endmodule

A control register block is a type of digital circuit that stores and controls the configuration of other circuits in a system. 
The block consists of a set of registers that are programmed to store the configuration settings, and a set of control signals that are used to apply the settings to the other circuits in the system.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a set of n control signals (ctrl1, ctrl2, ..., ctrln)
Outputs: a set of m configuration signals (cfg1, cfg2, ..., cfgm)
The module should also have the following parameters:

n: the number of control signals
m: the number of configuration signals
Your module should implement the following functionality:

The circuit should have n control signals that are used to program the registers in the block.
The circuit should have m configuration signals that are output by the block and used to control other circuits in the system.
To implement the control register block, you should use Verilog code to define the registers as a set of flip flops with synchronous reset and load inputs. 
You should then use the control signals to configure the flip flops with the desired settings.
Finally, you should use the output of the flip flops to generate the configuration signals that are used to control the other circuits in the system.
Response:
module control_reg_block (
  input [n-1:0] ctrl,
  output [m-1:0] cfg
);

parameter n = 4; // number of control signals
parameter m = 8; // number of configuration signals

reg [m-1:0] config_reg; // register to store configuration settings

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) begin // synchronous reset
    config_reg <= 0;
  end else if (load) begin // load input
    config_reg <= ctrl;
  end
end

assign cfg = config_reg; // output configuration signals

endmodule

The module should have the following outputs:

The opcode_inputs input will contain the opcode in the first 4 bits, followed by input A in the next 8 bits, and input B in the last 8 bits. The opcode can take on the following values:

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements edge detectors for both rising and falling edges of a signal. 
An edge detector is a digital circuit that detects a change in the input signal and outputs a pulse (e.g., a single clock cycle) in response.

You are tasked with designing a module that takes in 3 inputs, `A`, `B`, and `C`, and outputs `Y`. The output `Y` should be 1 if `A` is equal to `B` and `C` is equal to 0. Otherwise, the output `Y` should be 0. 

Design the module named `compare_abc` that implements this functionality. 

The module should have the following ports:
- `A` (input): a single bit input
- `B` (input): a single bit input
- `C` (input): a single bit input
- `Y` (output): a single bit output

Your design should be written in Verilog.
Response:
module compare_abc(
    input A,
    input B,
    input C,
    output reg Y
);

    always @(*) begin
        if(A == B && C == 0) begin
            Y = 1;
        end
        else begin
            Y = 0;
        end
    end

endmodule

You have been tasked with implementing a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) buffer using Verilog. Your FIFO buffer should have a depth of 128 elements, each element being 4 bits wide. The FIFO buffer should have two inputs, read and write, and two outputs, fifo_out and fifo_empty. The read and write inputs should be synchronous to a clock signal and the buffer should be resettable using a reset input. The fifo_out output should provide the data at the front of the buffer, while the fifo_empty output should indicate whether the buffer is empty or not.

Your Verilog module should have the following parameters:
- DEPTH: The depth of the FIFO buffer, set to 128.
- DEPTH_BINARY: The binary representation of the depth, set to 7 bits.
- WIDTH: The width of each element in the buffer, set to 4 bits.
- MAX_CONT: The maximum value that can be stored in the buffer, set to 127.

You should also define the following LED patterns as parameter values:
- reg0 to reg9: The LED patterns for the digits 0 to 9.
- rega to regf: The LED patterns for the letters A to F.

Your Verilog module should implement the following logic:
- The FIFO buffer should be initialized with all elements set to 0.
- When the read input is high and the write input is low, the data at the front of the buffer should be output on the fifo_out output.
- When the write input is high and the read input is low, the data on the fifo_in input should be written to the back of the buffer.
- When both the read and write inputs are high, the data on the fifo_in input should be written to the back of the buffer and the data at the front of the buffer should be output on the fifo_out output.
- The fifo_empty output should be high when the buffer is empty, and low otherwise.

Your Verilog module should be contained within 200 lines of code.
Response:
module fifo(clock, reset, read, write, fifo_in, fifo_out, fifo_empty, fifo_full);

    parameter DEPTH = 128;  						// 128 elements
    parameter DEPTH_BINARY = 7;  				// Binary representation of depth in 7 bits
    parameter WIDTH = 4;							// Each element is 4 bits
    parameter MAX_CONT = 7'b1111111;			// Maximum value that can be stored in the buffer, 127 [0~127]
    
    // LED patterns for hexadecimal digits
    parameter 
        reg0=7'b0000001,
        reg1=7'b1001111,
        reg2=7'b0010010,
        reg3=7'b0000110,
        reg4=7'b1001100,
        reg5=7'b0100100,
        reg6=7'b0100000,
        reg7=7'b0001101,
        reg8=7'b0000000,
        reg9=7'b0000100,
        rega=7'b0001000,
        regb=7'b1100000,
        regc=7'b0110001,
        regd=7'b1000010,
        rege=7'b0110000,
        regf=7'b0111000;
    
    input clock, reset, read, write;       			// Clock, reset, read and write inputs
    input [WIDTH-1:0] fifo_in;    					// Input data for FIFO 
    output [WIDTH-1:0] fifo_out;            	   // Output data from FIFO
    output fifo_empty, fifo_full;        			// Empty and full flags for FIFO

    reg [WIDTH-1:0] fifo_out;                    // Output data register
    reg [WIDTH-1:0] ram[DEPTH-1:0];              // RAM buffer of 128 elements, each 4 bits wide
    reg [DEPTH_BINARY-1:0] read_ptr, write_ptr, counter;        // Read and write pointers, and counter for buffer, 2^7 depth

    wire fifo_empty, fifo_full;          			// Empty and full flags for FIFO
    
    // Initialize FIFO buffer
    initial                                                
    begin             
        counter = 0;
        read_ptr = 0;
        write_ptr = 0;
        fifo_out = 0;
    end              
    
    // Empty and full flags for FIFO
    assign fifo_empty = (counter == 0);    		
    assign fifo_full = (counter == DEPTH-1);
    
    // Synchronous read and write operations for FIFO buffer
    always @(posedge clock)    						
    begin
        if (reset)   										// Reset FIFO buffer
        begin
            read_ptr = 0; 
            write_ptr = 0;
            counter = 0;
            fifo_out = 0;                    
        end
        else
        begin
            case ({read, write})  // Read and write operations
                2'b00:;  // No read or write operation
                2'b01:  // Write operation, input data written to back of buffer
                begin
                    if (counter < DEPTH - 1)	// Check if buffer is not full
                    begin
                        ram[write_ptr] = fifo_in;
                        counter = counter + 1;
                        write_ptr = (write_ptr == DEPTH-1) ? 0 : write_ptr + 1;
                    end
                end
                2'b10: // Read operation, data at front of buffer is output
                begin
                    if (counter > 0)	// Check if buffer is not empty
                    begin
                        fifo_out = ram[read_ptr];
                        counter = counter - 1;
                        read_ptr = (read_ptr == DEPTH-1) ? 0 : read_ptr + 1;
                    end
                end
                2'b11: // Read and write operation
                begin
                    if (counter == 0) // Buffer is empty, input data is output
                        fifo_out = fifo_in;
                    else // Buffer is not empty, input data is written to back of buffer and data at front of buffer is output
                    begin
                        ram[write_ptr] = fifo_in;
                        fifo_out = ram[read_ptr];
                        write_ptr = (write_ptr == DEPTH-1) ? 0 : write_ptr + 1;
                        read_ptr = (read_ptr == DEPTH-1) ? 0 : read_ptr + 1;
                    end
                end
            endcase
        end
    end
    
endmodule

module shift_register (

    input rst,
    input [3:0] shift_in,
    output reg [3:0] shift_out
);

Outputs: a signal y that represents the resulting angle in radians

You should then use these functions to compute the resulting angle in radians and output the result.

Here are the formulas for the three inverse trigonometric functions:

- arcsine(x) = sin^-1(x)
- arccosine(x) = cos^-1(x)
- arctangent(x) = tan^-1(x)

To implement these formulas, you can use the built-in Verilog functions for sine, cosine, and tangent, as well as the pi constant. 

To finish this task, you need to define the module name as well as input and output definitions. 
You should also define any necessary parameters, such as the precision of the output or any scaling factors. 
Then, you should define the mathematical formulas for the three inverse trigonometric functions and use them to compute the result. 
Finally, you should output the result to the y signal.

module inv_trig (
  input x, // value to compute the inverse trigonometric function
  output y // resulting angle in radians
);

  parameter PRECISION = 16; // number of bits for the output precision
  parameter SCALE_FACTOR = 2**PRECISION / (2 * $pi); // scaling factor for the output
  
  reg signed [PRECISION-1:0] y_reg; // register to hold the output value
  
  always @(*) begin
    if (x >= 1) begin
      y_reg = $signed(0); // if x is greater than or equal to 1, output pi/2
    end else if (x <= -1) begin
      y_reg = $signed(-$pi/2); // if x is less than or equal to -1, output -pi/2
    end else begin
      y_reg = $signed($asin(x)); // compute arcsine of x and store in y_reg
    end
  end
  
  assign y = y_reg * SCALE_FACTOR; // scale the output value and assign to y
  
endmodule

);

(

    input clk,
    output reg [n-1:0] count
);

  input CLOCKENABLE,
  input DOUT0,
  input DOUT1,
  input INPUTCLK,
  input LATCHINPUTVALUE,
  input OUTPUTCLK,
  input OUTPUTENABLE,
  output reg DIN0,

  input clk,
  input tone_sel,
  output reg tone_out
);

parameter tone_frequency = 1000; // frequency of the tone
parameter tone_duration = 100; // duration of the tone in clock cycles (assuming a 1 kHz clock)

reg [31:0] duration_counter;

module bitwise_op (

    input [7:0] B,
    input [2:0] ctrl,
    output reg [7:0] out

        case(ctrl)

module no_input_circuit (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  output reg out
);

  parameter S0 = 2'b00; // initial state
  parameter S1 = 2'b01; // state to output 1
  parameter S2 = 2'b10; // state to output 0

  reg [1:0] state; // current state of the FSM

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
      state <= S0; // reset to initial state
      out <= 0; // output 0
    end else begin
      case (state)
        S0: begin
          state <= S1; // go to output 1 state
          out <= 1; // output 1
        end
        S1: begin
          if (state == 10) begin
            state <= S2; // go to output 0 state
            out <= 0; // output 0
          end else begin
            state <= state + 1; // increment state
            out <= 1; // output 1
          end
        end
        S2: begin
          state <= S2; // stay in output 0 state
          out <= 0; // output 0
        end
      endcase
    end
  end

endmodule

module top_module (
    input clk,
    input rst_n,
    input [7:0] data_in_1,
    input [7:0] data_in_2,
    input valid_a,
    input ready_b,
    output ready_a,
    output reg valid_b,
    output reg [9:0] data_out
);

// Instantiate the accumulator module
accumulator_module accumulator (
    .clk(clk),
    .rst_n(rst_n),
    .data_in_1(data_in_1),
    .data_in_2(data_in_2),
    .valid_a(valid_a),
    .ready_a(ready_a),
    .valid_b(valid_b),
    .data_out(data_out[7:0])
);

// Instantiate the half adder module
half_adder_module half_adder (
    .a(data_out[0]),
    .b(data_out[1]),
    .sum(data_out[8]),
    .carry_out(data_out[9])
);

// Valid-ready handshake
always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (rst_n == 0) begin
        valid_b <= 0;
    end else begin
        if (valid_a && ready_b) begin
            valid_b <= 1;
        end else begin
            valid_b <= 0;
        end
    end
end

endmodule

A sequence detector state machine is a type of digital circuit that can detect a specific pattern of input signals. 
The inputs to the circuit are a sequence of binary signals, and the circuit should output a signal when it detects the specific pattern.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

sequence: the specific pattern to detect

The circuit should be implemented using a state machine that has n states, where each state represents a different position in the input sequence.
To implement the state machine, you should use Verilog code to define the transition logic between states based on the input signal. 
You should also define the output logic to output a signal when the sequence is detected.

module seq_detector (
  input in,
  output reg out
);

parameter n = 4; // number of bits in the input sequence
parameter sequence = 4'b1101; // specific pattern to detect

reg [n-1:0] state; // state register
reg [n-1:0] seq_reg; // sequence register

always @(posedge in) begin
  seq_reg <= {seq_reg[n-2:0], in}; // shift in new input
  case (state)
    0: if (seq_reg == sequence) begin
         out <= 1; // output signal when sequence is detected
         state <= n-1; // transition to final state
       end else begin
         out <= 0;
         state <= 0; // reset to initial state
       end
    default: if (seq_reg == sequence) begin
               out <= 1; // output signal when sequence is detected
               state <= n-1; // transition to final state
             end else begin
               out <= 0;
               state <= state - 1; // transition to next state
             end
  endcase
end

endmodule

- `reg_addr`: the address of the register being accessed
- `reg_wr_data`: the data to be written to the register (if the operation is a write)
- `reg_rd_data`: the data read from the register (if the operation is a read)
- `reg_ack`: a signal indicating that the register operation has been acknowledged

The module should have the following behavior:
- On reset, the `reg_rd_data` output should be set to 0 and the `reg_ack` output should be deasserted.
- When a register read or write request is made (`reg_req` is high):
  - If the register address is invalid (i.e. outside the range of valid addresses), the `reg_ack` output should be deasserted and the `reg_rd_data` output should be set to 0.
  - If the register address is valid:
    - If the operation is a write, the `reg_ack` output should be asserted and the data should be written to the register.
    - If the operation is a read, the `reg_ack` output should be asserted and the data from the register should be output on `reg_rd_data`.

module register_interface (
  input wire reset,
  input wire clk,
  input wire reg_req,
  input wire reg_rd_wr_L,
  input wire [7:0] reg_addr,
  input wire [31:0] reg_wr_data,
  output reg [31:0] reg_rd_data,
  output reg reg_ack
);

  reg [31:0] register [255:0]; // 256 registers, each 32 bits wide

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
      reg_rd_data <= 0;
      reg_ack <= 0;
    end
    else if (reg_req) begin
      if (reg_addr > 255) begin // invalid address
        reg_rd_data <= 0;
        reg_ack <= 0;
      end
      else begin // valid address
        if (reg_rd_wr_L) begin // write operation
          register[reg_addr] <= reg_wr_data;
          reg_ack <= 1;
        end
        else begin // read operation
          reg_rd_data <= register[reg_addr];
          reg_ack <= 1;
        end
      end
    end
  end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements an asynchronous reset release circuit. 
An asynchronous reset is a signal that resets a circuit to a known state when it is asserted. 
However, when the reset signal is deasserted, the circuit may take some time to release from the reset state and start functioning properly. 
An asynchronous reset release circuit is used to ensure that the circuit is released from the reset state as quickly as possible.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- reset: an asynchronous reset signal
- clk: a clock signal
Outputs: 
- release: a signal that indicates when the circuit has been released from the reset state

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- When the reset signal is asserted, the release signal should be low.
- When the reset signal is deasserted, the release signal should remain low for a specified release time.
- After the release time has elapsed, the release signal should go high to indicate that the circuit has been released from the reset state.
- When the reset signal is asserted again, the release signal should immediately go low.

To implement the asynchronous reset release circuit, you should use Verilog code to define a counter that counts clock cycles and a comparator that compares the counter value to the release time. 
When the reset signal is asserted, the counter should be reset to zero. 
When the reset signal is deasserted, the counter should start counting the clock cycles. 
When the counter value is equal to the release time, the release signal should go high.

module async_reset_release (
  input reset,
  input clk,
  output release
);

  parameter RELEASE_TIME = 10; // Release time in clock cycles

  reg [7:0] counter; // 8-bit counter for counting clock cycles
  reg release_reg; // Register for storing release signal

  always @(posedge clk or negedge reset) begin
    if (reset == 0) begin
      counter <= 0; // Reset counter to zero
      release_reg <= 0; // Set release signal to low
    end
    else begin
      if (counter == RELEASE_TIME) begin
        release_reg <= 1; // Set release signal to high
      end
      else begin
        release_reg <= 0; // Set release signal to low
      end
      
      if (release_reg == 0) begin
        counter <= counter + 1; // Increment counter if release signal is low
      end
    end
  end

  assign release = release_reg;

endmodule

The system should have one input port for the clock signal, and one input port for the reset signal. module binary_sequence (
  input [7:0] data_in, // 8-bit input data 
  input clk, // Clock signal input 
  input rst_n, // Active low synchronous reset input 
  output reg [7:0] final_out // 8-bit output from bitwise AND operation 
);

  reg [63:0] shift_reg; // 64-bit shift register 
  reg [2:0] counter; // 3-bit counter for sequence generation 

  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (~rst_n) begin
      shift_reg <= 64'b0;
      counter <= 3'b0;
      final_out <= 8'b0;
    end
    else begin
      shift_reg <= {shift_reg[62:0], counter}; // Shift in counter value 
      counter <= counter + 1; // Increment counter 
      final_out <= shift_reg[63:56] & data_in; // Perform bitwise AND operation 
    end
  end

endmodule

module top_module (
  input clk, // Clock signal input 
  input rst_n, // Active low synchronous reset input 
  input [63:0] SR_out, // 64-bit output from shift register 
  output reg [7:0] final_out // 8-bit output from bitwise AND operation 
);

  wire [7:0] data_in = 8'b11111111; // Set input data to all 1's 

  binary_sequence seq_gen (
    .data_in(data_in),
    .clk(clk),
    .rst_n(rst_n),
    .final_out(final_out)
  );

  assign SR_out = seq_gen.shift_reg; // Connect shift register output to top module output 

endmodule

A power-on reset generator is a type of digital circuit that generates a reset signal when power is first applied to the circuit. 
The reset signal is used to initialize the circuit to a known state, ensuring that it starts up in a predictable way.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

module POR (
  input vdd, // power supply signal
  input clk, // clock signal
  output reg rst // reset signal
);

  reg [23:0] counter; // 24-bit counter for delay time
  
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (vdd == 1'b0) begin // power removed
      rst <= 1'b1; // set reset signal high
      counter <= 0; // reset counter
    end
    else if (counter == 24'd100000) begin // delay time elapsed
      rst <= 1'b0; // set reset signal low
    end
    else begin // count up
      counter <= counter + 1;
    end
  end
  
endmodule

module counter (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input enable,
  output reg [3:0] count
);

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) begin
    count <= 4'b0000;
  end else if (enable) begin
    if (count == 4'b1010) begin
      count <= 4'b0000;
    end else begin
      count <= count + 1;
    end
  end
end

endmodule

You are tasked with designing a BusReader module that interfaces with a bus and provides data to a client module. The BusReader module should have the following parameters:

- bus_width: The width of the bus data in bits. The default value is 32.
- bus_max_devices: The maximum number of devices on the bus. The default value is 16.
- bus_buffer_size: The size of the buffer FIFOs. The default value is 32.
- device_id: The ID of the device that the BusReader module is servicing. This should be a bit position in bus_voice or bus_receiver. The default value is 1.

The BusReader module should have the following inputs and outputs:

- Inputs:
  - clk: The clock signal.
  - bus_data: The data on the bus.
  - bus_receiver: A bus_max_devices-bit vector indicating which devices are receivers of the current bus transaction.
  - bus_voice: A bus_max_devices-bit vector indicating which devices are talking on the bus.
- Outputs:
  - client_data: The data to be provided to the client module.
  - client_source_addr: A bus_max_devices-bit vector indicating the source address of the data.
  - bus_buffer_full: A bus_max_devices-bit vector indicating whether the buffer FIFOs are full.
  - client_buffer_empty: A boolean indicating whether the client_data buffer FIFO is empty.
  - client_buffer_full: A boolean indicating whether the client_data buffer FIFO is full.

The BusReader module should function as follows:

- If the current bus transaction is not addressed to the device with ID device_id, the BusReader module should do nothing.
- If the current bus transaction is addressed to the device with ID device_id and the device with ID device_id is not talking on the bus, the BusReader module should store the data in the client_data buffer FIFO and the source address in the client_source_addr buffer FIFO.
- If the current bus transaction is addressed to the device with ID device_id and the device with ID device_id is talking on the bus, the BusReader module should do nothing.

The BusReader module should also display an error message if it receives data from address 0.
Response:
module BusReader
#(
    parameter bus_width=32,
    parameter bus_max_devices=16,
    parameter bus_buffer_size=32,
    parameter device_id=1
)
(
    input clk,
    input [bus_width-1:0] bus_data,
    input [bus_max_devices-1:0] bus_receiver,
    output [bus_max_devices-1:0] bus_buffer_full,
    input  [bus_max_devices-1:0] bus_voice,
    output reg [bus_width-1:0] client_data,
    output reg [bus_max_devices-1:0] client_source_addr,
    input client_next,
    output reg client_buffer_empty,
    output reg client_buffer_full
);

    reg data_on_bus=bus_receiver[device_id] && bus_voice;
    assign bus_buffer_full[device_id]=client_buffer_full;

    reg clear=0;

    FIFO
    #(
        .data_width(bus_width),
        .size(bus_buffer_size),
        .device_id(device_id)
    ) buffer
    (   
        .data_in(bus_data),
        .data_out(client_data),
        .clk(clk),
        .next(client_next),
        .insert(data_on_bus),
        .clear(clear),
        .full(client_buffer_full),
        .empty(client_buffer_empty)
    );
    
    reg sender_addresses_buffer_full;
    reg sender_addresses_buffer_empty;

    FIFO
    #(
        .data_width(bus_max_devices), 
        .size(bus_buffer_size),
        .device_id(device_id<<1)
    ) sender_addresses
    (
        .data_in(bus_voice),
        .data_out(client_source_addr),
        .clk(clk),
        .next(client_next),
        .insert(data_on_bus),
        .clear(clear),
        .full(sender_addresses_buffer_full),
        .empty(sender_addresses_buffer_empty)
    );

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (data_on_bus && client_source_addr==0)
            $display("BusReader %d: --MAJOR SCREWUP-- Received data from address 0",device_id);
    end
endmodule

module binary_counter (
    input clk,
    input ena,
    input rst,
    input [3:0] test,
    output reg [3:0] count,
    output max_reached
);

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (rst) begin
        count <= 4'b0;
        max_reached <= 1'b0;
    end
    else if (ena) begin
        count <= count + 1;
        if (count == 4'b1111) begin
            max_reached <= 1'b1;
        end
        else begin
            max_reached <= 1'b0;
        end
    end
end

Design a system that combines the 4-bit magnitude comparator and 4-bit binary counter modules. The system should include an additional functional module that takes in both the 2-bit output from the comparator and the 4-bit output from the counter to determine the final output value. If the comparator output is 00, the final output should be the counter output shifted left by 4 bits. If the comparator output is 01, the final output should be the counter output shifted left by 2 bits. If the comparator output is 10, the final output should be the counter output shifted right by 2 bits. If the comparator output is 11, the final output should be the counter output shifted right by 4 bits. The system should have a synchronous active-high reset that resets the counter and the functional module to zero. The system should also have a select input that enables either the comparator or the counter. The output should be the active module's value.

module magnitude_comparator (
    input [3:0] A,
    input [3:0] B,
    input [3:0] C,
    input [3:0] D,
    output reg [1:0] out
);

always @(*) begin
    if (A > B && C > D) begin
        out = 2'b00; // A > B and C > D
    end else if (A < B && C < D) begin
        out = 2'b11; // A < B and C < D
    end else if (A > B && C < D) begin
        out = 2'b01; // A > B and C < D
    end else if (A < B && C > D) begin
        out = 2'b10; // A < B and C > D
    end
end

endmodule

module binary_counter (
    input clk,
    input EN,
    input RST,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (RST) begin
        count <= 4'b0000;
    end else if (EN) begin
        count <= count + 1;
    end
end

endmodule

module functional_module (
    input [1:0] comparator_out,
    input [3:0] counter_out,
    output reg [7:0] out
);

always @(*) begin
    case (comparator_out)
        2'b00: out = {counter_out, 4'b0000}; // Shift left by 4 bits
        2'b01: out = {counter_out, 2'b00, 2'b00}; // Shift left by 2 bits
        2'b10: out = {2'b00, counter_out[3:0]}; // Shift right by 2 bits
        2'b11: out = {4'b0000, counter_out}; // Shift right by 4 bits
    endcase
end

endmodule

module top_module (
    input clk,
    input reset,      // Synchronous active-high reset
    input [3:0] A,    // Input A for the magnitude comparator
    input [3:0] B,    // Input B for the magnitude comparator
    input [3:0] C,    // Input C for the magnitude comparator
    input [3:0] D,    // Input D for the magnitude comparator
    input select,     // Select input to choose between the comparator and the counter
    input EN,         // Enable input for the binary counter
    input RST,        // Asynchronous reset input for the binary counter
    output reg [7:0] q // 8-bit output from the active module
);

wire [1:0] comparator_out;
wire [3:0] counter_out;

magnitude_comparator comparator(.A(A), .B(B), .C(C), .D(D), .out(comparator_out));
binary_counter counter(.clk(clk), .EN(EN), .RST(RST), .count(counter_out));
functional_module functional(.comparator_out(comparator_out), .counter_out(counter_out), .out(q));

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
        q <= 8'b0;
    end else if (select) begin
        q <= comparator_out;
    end else begin
        q <= functional.out;
    end
end

endmodule

The module should be able to control the movement of the elevator car based on the current floor, direction, and destination. The elevator car driver should be able to move up or down, stop at requested floors, and reach the final destination. 

The elevator car driver module should take in four inputs: 
- `current_floor` (a 4-bit input) represents the current floor of the elevator car.
- `direction` (a 1-bit input) represents the direction of the elevator car. A value of 0 represents the elevator car moving down, and a value of 1 represents the elevator car moving up.
- `destination` (a 4-bit input) represents the final destination floor of the elevator car.
- `clock` (a 1-bit input) represents the clock signal.

The elevator car driver module should have two outputs:
- `floor` (a 4-bit output) represents the current floor of the elevator car.
- `course` (a 1-bit output) represents the direction of the elevator car. A value of 0 represents the elevator car moving down, and a value of 1 represents the elevator car moving up.

The elevator car driver module should be able to move the elevator car based on the following rules:
- If the elevator car is already at the destination floor, it should stop.
- If the elevator car is not at the destination floor, it should move in the direction of the destination floor.
- If the elevator car reaches a floor where someone has requested to stop, it should stop and open the doors.

module elevator_car_driver(current_floor, direction, destination, clock, floor, course);

    parameter FLOOR_NUM = 16; // number of floors
    parameter DOOR_OPEN_TIME = 10; // door open time in clock cycles
    
    input [3:0] current_floor;
    input direction;
    input [3:0] destination;
    input clock;
    
    output reg [3:0] floor;
    output reg course;
    
    reg [3:0] target; // target floor
    reg door_open; // flag to indicate if the door is open
    reg [7:0] door_open_timer; // timer for the door to stay open
    
    always @(posedge clock) begin
        if (door_open) begin // if the door is open
            door_open_timer <= door_open_timer + 1; // increment the timer
            if (door_open_timer == DOOR_OPEN_TIME) begin // if the timer has reached the door open time
                door_open <= 0; // close the door
                door_open_timer <= 0; // reset the timer
            end
        end else begin // if the door is closed
            if (current_floor == target) begin // if the elevator car has reached the target floor
                course <= 0; // stop the elevator car
                floor <= current_floor; // set the current floor
                door_open <= 1; // open the door
            end else begin // if the elevator car has not reached the target floor yet
                floor <= current_floor; // set the current floor
                if (direction) begin // if the elevator car is moving up
                    if (current_floor < target) begin // if the elevator car has not reached the target floor yet
                        course <= 1; // set the course to up
                        floor <= floor + 1; // move the elevator car up
                    end else begin // if the elevator car has reached the target floor
                        course <= 0; // stop the elevator car
                        door_open <= 1; // open the door
                    end
                end else begin // if the elevator car is moving down
                    if (current_floor > target) begin // if the elevator car has not reached the target floor yet
                        course <= 0; // set the course to down
                        floor <= floor - 1; // move the elevator car down
                    end else begin // if the elevator car has reached the target floor
                        course <= 0; // stop the elevator car
                        door_open <= 1; // open the door
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end
    
    always @(posedge clock) begin
        if (current_floor == destination) begin // if the elevator car has reached the final destination
            target <= current_floor; // set the target to the current floor
        end else begin // if the elevator car has not reached the final destination yet
            target <= destination; // set the target to the final destination
        end
    end
    
endmodule

- When the "load" input is high, the "count" output should be set to the value of the "increment" input.
- When neither "reset" nor "load" is high, the "count" output should be incremented by the value of the "increment" input on every clock cycle.

Assume that the input values will be stable for at least one clock cycle before the next clock edge.

module counter (
    input clk,
    input [3:0] reset,
    input [3:0] load,
    input [3:0] increment,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset == 4'b1111) begin
        count <= 4'b0000;
    end else if (load != 4'b0000) begin
        count <= load;
    end else begin
        count <= count + increment;
    end
end

endmodule

   input        reset_n,
   input        test_panel_select_n,

   input        load_led_vals,

   input [7:0]  pwm_time,

);

  input         clk125,
  output        clk,
  output        clk_locked
);

  wire        clk_clk_gen;
  wire        clk_locked_int;
  wire        clkfbout_clk_gen;

  MMCME2_ADV
  #(.BANDWIDTH            ("HIGH"),
    .CLKOUT4_CASCADE      ("FALSE"),
    .COMPENSATION         ("ZHOLD"),
    .STARTUP_WAIT         ("FALSE"),
    .DIVCLK_DIVIDE        (12),
    .CLKFBOUT_MULT_F      (40),

    .CLKOUT0_DIVIDE_F     (400),

    .CLKOUT0_DUTY_CYCLE   (0.500),
    .CLKOUT0_USE_FINE_PS  ("FALSE"),
    .CLKIN1_PERIOD        (8.0))
  mmcm_adv_inst
    (
    .CLKFBOUT            (clkfbout_clk_gen),
    .CLKOUT0             (clk_clk_gen),
    .CLKIN1              (clk125),
    .CLKINSEL            (1'b1),
    .LOCKED              (clk_locked_int)
    );

  assign clk_locked = clk_locked_int;
  BUFG clk_buf (.O(clk), .I(clk_clk_gen));

endmodule

The Verilog module should be named `macc_module` and should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:
- `clk`: a clock signal
- `reset`: a reset signal that resets the accumulated value to 0
- `a`: a 32-bit integer
- `b`: a 32-bit integer

Outputs:
- `out`: a 32-bit integer representing the result of the MACC operation

The module should implement the following behavior:
- On the rising edge of `clk`, if `reset` is high, the accumulated value should be set to 0
- On the rising edge of `clk`, the module should multiply `a` and `b` and add the result to the accumulated value
- On the next rising edge of `clk`, the output `out` should be updated with the accumulated value

You may assume that the inputs `a` and `b` will not change during a single clock cycle.

module macc_module(
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input [31:0] a,
  input [31:0] b,
  output [31:0] out
);

  reg [31:0] accum; // register to hold accumulated value

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
      accum <= 0;
    end else begin
      accum <= accum + (a * b);
    end
  end

  assign out = accum;

endmodule

module calculator(
    input wire signed [31:0] a,
    input wire signed [31:0] b,
    input wire [1:0] op,
    input wire ready,
    output reg signed [31:0] result
);
    always @(*) begin
        if (ready) begin
            case (op)
                2'b00: result = a + b; // addition
                2'b01: result = a - b; // subtraction
                2'b10: result = a * b; // multiplication
                2'b11: result = a / b; // division
            endcase
        end
    end
endmodule

module synchronous_reset (
    input wire clk,
    input wire out,
    input wire in0,
    output reg AS
);

            AS <= out;

module ram (
  input  [ 8:0] RAM_P0_ADDR,
  input         RAM_P0_CLK,
  input         RAM_P0_CLKS,
  input  [ 3:0] RAM_P0_WR_BE,
  input  [31:0] RAM_P0_WR_DATA,
  input         RAM_P0_WR_EN,
  input  [ 8:0] RAM_P1_ADDR,
  input         RAM_P1_CLK,
  input         RAM_P1_CLKS,
  output [31:0] RAM_P1_RD_DATA,
  input         RAM_P1_RD_EN,
  input         RAM_RME_af,
  input  [ 3:0] RAM_RM_af,
  input         RAM_TEST1_af
);

  reg [31:0] mem [511:0]; // 512 x 32-bit memory

  always @(posedge RAM_P0_CLK or posedge RAM_P0_CLKS) begin
    if (RAM_RME_af) begin
      if (RAM_RM_af == 1) begin
        // Asynchronous reset
        mem <= 'bx;
      end else if (RAM_RM_af == 2) begin
        // Synchronous reset
        if (RAM_P0_CLKS) begin
          mem <= 'bx;
        end
      end
    end else if (RAM_P0_WR_EN) begin
      // Write operation
      mem[RAM_P0_ADDR] <= {mem[RAM_P0_ADDR][31:8*RAM_P0_WR_BE], RAM_P0_WR_DATA[31:8*RAM_P0_WR_BE]};
    end
  end

  always @(posedge RAM_P1_CLK or posedge RAM_P1_CLKS) begin
    if (RAM_RME_af) begin
      if (RAM_RM_af == 1) begin
        // Asynchronous reset
        RAM_P1_RD_DATA <= 'bx;
      end else if (RAM_RM_af == 2) begin
        // Synchronous reset
        if (RAM_P1_CLKS) begin
          RAM_P1_RD_DATA <= 'bx;
        end
      end
    end else if (RAM_P1_RD_EN) begin
      // Read operation
      RAM_P1_RD_DATA <= mem[RAM_P1_ADDR];
    end

endmodule

    parameter RAMTYPE = "RAM_BLOCK_TYPE=M512",
    parameter USEEAB = "ON"
) (
    input aclr,
    input clock,
    input [107:0] data,
    input rdreq,
    input wrreq,
    output almost_empty,
    output almost_full,
    output empty,
    output full,
    output [107:0] q
);

    wire sub_wire0;
    wire sub_wire1;
    wire sub_wire2;
    wire [107:0] sub_wire3;
    wire sub_wire4;

    scfifo #(
        .add_ram_output_register("ON"),
        .almost_empty_value(5),
        .almost_full_value(10),
        .intended_device_family("Stratix II GX"),
        .lpm_hint(RAMTYPE),
        .lpm_numwords(16),
        .lpm_showahead("OFF"),
        .lpm_type("scfifo"),
        .lpm_width(108),
        .lpm_widthu(4),
        .overflow_checking("OFF"),
        .underflow_checking("OFF"),
        .use_eab(USEEAB)
    ) scfifo_component (
        .rdreq(rdreq),
        .aclr(aclr),
        .clock(clock),
        .wrreq(wrreq),
        .data(data),
        .almost_full(sub_wire0),
        .empty(sub_wire1),
        .almost_empty(sub_wire2),
        .q(sub_wire3),
        .full(sub_wire4),
        .sclr(),
        .usedw()
    );

    assign almost_empty = sub_wire2;
    assign empty = sub_wire1;
    assign almost_full = sub_wire0;
    assign full = sub_wire4;
    assign q = sub_wire3;

endmodule

Memory protection blocks are used to protect memory regions from unwanted access, such as write or read operations. 
In this task, you will create a memory protection block that will only allow read access to a specific memory region.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- clk: a clock signal
- rst: a reset signal
- read_en: a read enable signal
- addr: a memory address signal
- data_in: a data input signal

Outputs: 
- data_out: a data output signal
- read_ok: a signal indicating whether the read operation was successful or not

The module should also have the following parameters:
- mem_size: the size of the memory region to be protected
- mem_start: the starting address of the memory region to be protected

Your module should implement the following functionality:
- The module should have a memory region of size mem_size, starting at address mem_start, that can only be read.
- If the read_en signal is high, the module should output the data at the memory address specified by the addr input signal.
- If the read_en signal is low, the module should output 0.
- If the memory address specified by the addr input signal is outside the memory region to be protected, the read_ok signal should be low.
- If the memory address specified by the addr input signal is inside the memory region to be protected, the read_ok signal should be high.

To implement the memory protection block, you should use Verilog code to define the memory region as a range of memory addresses. 
You should then use conditional statements to check if the memory address specified by the addr input signal is inside or outside the memory region to be protected. 
Finally, you should use the read_en signal to control whether the data at the memory address should be outputted or not.

module mem_protect (
  input clk,
  input rst,
  input read_en,
  input [7:0] addr,
  input [7:0] data_in,
  output [7:0] data_out,
  output read_ok
);

parameter mem_size = 64; // size of memory region to be protected
parameter mem_start = 128; // starting address of memory region to be protected

reg [7:0] memory [mem_start + mem_size - 1:mem_start]; // define memory region

assign read_ok = (addr >= mem_start) && (addr < mem_start + mem_size); // check if address is within memory region

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin
    data_out <= 0;
  end else begin
    if (read_en && read_ok) begin
      data_out <= memory[addr - mem_start];
    end else begin
      data_out <= 0;
    end
  end
end

endmodule

The following operations should be supported by the ALU:

- Subtraction (FS = 00001)
- Bitwise AND (FS = 00010)
- Bitwise OR (FS = 00011)
- Bitwise XOR (FS = 00100)
- Logical left shift (FS = 00101)
- Logical right shift (FS = 00110)

module ALU_Cell_4bit(
    input wire A_from_next_bit,
    input wire C_in,
    input wire [3:0] A,
    input wire [3:0] B,
    input wire [4:0] FS,
    output wire C_out,
    output wire [3:0] F
);

wire [3:0] F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED;
wire SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_0;
wire SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_1;
wire SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_2;

// Arithmetic operations
assign F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[0] = (FS == 5'b00000) ? A + B : // Addition
                                (FS == 5'b00001) ? A - B : // Subtraction
                                (FS == 5'b00101) ? {A[2:0], 3'b000} : // Logical left shift
                                (FS == 5'b00110) ? {2'b00, A[3:1]} : // Logical right shift
                                4'bzzzz; // Undefined

// Logical operations
assign F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[1] = (FS == 5'b00010) ? A & B : // Bitwise AND
                                (FS == 5'b00011) ? A | B : // Bitwise OR
                                (FS == 5'b00100) ? A ^ B : // Bitwise XOR
                                4'bzzzz; // Undefined

// Generate carry out
assign C_out = (FS == 5'b00000 && (A[3] & B[3])) || // Addition
               (FS == 5'b00001 && (A[3] < B[3] || (A[3] == B[3] && A < B))) || // Subtraction
               1'b0; // No carry out for logical operations

// Instantiate ALU_Cell_1bit modules for each bit
ALU_Cell_1bit b2v_inst0 (
    .A(A[0]),
    .B(B[0]),
    .C_in(C_in),
    .A_from_next_bit(A_from_next_bit),
    .FS(FS),
    .F(F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[0]),
    .C_out(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_1)
);

ALU_Cell_1bit b2v_inst1 (
    .A(A[1]),
    .B(B[1]),
    .C_in(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_1),
    .A_from_next_bit(A[2]),
    .FS(FS),
    .F(F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[1]),
    .C_out(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_2)
);

ALU_Cell_1bit b2v_inst2 (
    .A(A[2]),
    .B(B[2]),
    .C_in(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_2),
    .A_from_next_bit(A[3]),
    .FS(FS),
    .F(F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[2]),
    .C_out(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_0)
);

ALU_Cell_1bit b2v_inst3 (
    .A(A[3]),
    .B(B[3]),
    .C_in(SYNTHESIZED_WIRE_0),
    .A_from_next_bit(A_from_next_bit),
    .FS(FS),
    .F(F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED[3]),
    .C_out(C_out)
);

// Assign output
assign F = F_ALTERA_SYNTHESIZED;

endmodule

A POR generator is a circuit that ensures that all flip-flops in a digital system are reset to a known state when the system is powered on.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

After the fixed period of time has elapsed, the reset signal should be de-asserted.
The reset signal should also be asserted whenever the clock signal transitions from low to high (i.e., on the rising edge of the clock signal).
To implement the POR generator, you should use Verilog code to generate a pulse of fixed duration when the power-on signal is asserted. 
You should then use this pulse to assert the reset signal for the fixed period of time. 
You should also use the clock signal to generate a pulse on the rising edge of the clock signal, which should also assert the reset signal.
Finally, you should use a flip-flop to synchronize the reset signal with the clock signal.

module POR (
  input clk,
  input por,
  output reg rst
);

parameter n = 8; // number of flip-flops

reg [7:0] counter; // counter for fixed duration pulse

// Verilog code for generating a pulse of fixed duration
// when the power-on signal is asserted
always @(posedge por) begin
  counter <= 8'hFF; // set counter to maximum value
end

// Verilog code for generating a pulse on the rising edge of the clock signal
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (counter > 0) begin
    rst <= 1; // assert reset signal
    counter <= counter - 1; // decrement counter
  end else begin
    rst <= 0; // de-assert reset signal
  end
end

// Verilog code for synchronizing the reset signal with the clock signal
always @(posedge clk) begin
  rst <= por || rst; // OR the reset signal with the power-on signal
end

endmodule

- After every clock cycle, toggle the least significant bit of `count`

- After the sixth iteration, reset `count` to `00000001` and repeat the entire pattern again

module binary_sequence(output reg [7:0] count, input clk, reset);
    reg [3:0] state; // 0 to 13 needed.

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset == 1) begin
            state = 13;
            count = 8'b00000010;
        end
        else begin
            case(state)
                0: begin count <= 8'b00000010; state <= 1; end
                1: begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 2; end
                2: begin count <= {count[6:0], count[7]}; state <= 3; end
                3: begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 4; end
                4: begin count <= {count[5:0], count[7:6]}; state <= 5; end
                5: begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 6; end

                8: begin count <= {count[3:0], count[7:4]}; state <= 9; end
                9: begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 10;end
                10:begin count <= {count[2:0], count[7:3]}; state <= 11;end
                11:begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 12;end
                12:begin count <= {count[1:0], count[7:2]}; state <= 13;end
                13,14,15:
                   begin count[0] <= ~count[0]; state <= 0; end
            endcase

    input clk,
    input reset,
    input load,
    input [3:0] data_in,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

always @(posedge clk or negedge reset) begin
    if (!reset) begin
        count <= 4'b0;
    end else if (load) begin
        count <= data_in;
    end else begin
        count <= count + 1;
    end
end

module barrel_shifter_4bit (
    input [3:0] in,
    input [1:0] shift,
    output reg [3:0] out
);

    always @(*) begin
        case(shift)
            2'b00: out = in << 1; // logical left shift
            2'b01: out = in >> 1; // logical right shift
            2'b10: out = {in[2], in[3], in[3], in[3]}; // arithmetic left shift
            2'b11: out = {in[3], in[3], in[3], in[2]}; // arithmetic right shift
            default: out = 4'b0; // default case

    end

endmodule

module apu_div
#(
  parameter PERIOD_BITS = 16
)
(
  input  wire                   clk_in,     // system clock signal
  input  wire                   rst_in,     // reset signal
  input  wire                   pulse_in,   // input pulse
  input  wire                   reload_in,  // reset counter to period_in (no pulse_out generated)
  input  wire [PERIOD_BITS-1:0] period_in,  // new period value
  output wire                   pulse_out   // divided output pulse
);

reg  [PERIOD_BITS-1:0] q_cnt;
wire [PERIOD_BITS-1:0] d_cnt;

always @(posedge clk_in)
  begin
    if (rst_in)
      q_cnt <= 0;
    else
      q_cnt <= d_cnt;

assign d_cnt     = (reload_in || (pulse_in && (q_cnt == 0))) ? period_in    :
                   (pulse_in)                                ? q_cnt - 1'h1 : q_cnt;
assign pulse_out = pulse_in && (q_cnt == 0);

endmodule

);
