module rotator (
    input clk,        // System clock
    input reset,      // Synchronous active-high reset
    input [99:0] data,// 100-bit input for the rotator
    input [1:0] shift,// 2-bit input to select shift direction
    output [99:0] out // 100-bit output from the rotator
);

reg [99:0] shift_reg;   // Register to hold shifted data

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
        shift_reg <= 100'b0;    // Reset to 0
    end else begin
        case (shift)
            2'b00: shift_reg <= {shift_reg[98:0], data[99]};   // Left shift
            2'b01: shift_reg <= {data[0], shift_reg[99:1]};     // Right shift
            default: shift_reg <= shift_reg;                   // No shift
        endcase
    end
end

assign out = shift_reg;     // Assign shifted data to output

endmodule

module counter (
    input clk,          // System clock
    input reset,        // Synchronous active-high reset
    output reg [3:0] out // 4-bit output from the counter
);

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
        out <= 4'b0;    // Reset to 0
    end else begin
        out <= out + 1; // Increment counter
    end
end

endmodule

module control_logic (
    input [1:0] select,             // Select input to choose between rotator and counter
    input [99:0] rotator_data,      // 100-bit input for the rotator
    input [3:0] counter_data,       // 4-bit input for the counter
    output [99:0] rotator_out,      // 100-bit output from the rotator
    output [3:0] counter_out        // 4-bit output from the counter
);

wire [99:0] rotator_out_wire;      // Wire to hold rotator output
wire [3:0] counter_out_wire;       // Wire to hold counter output

rotator rotator_inst (
    .clk(clk),
    .reset(reset),
    .data(rotator_data),
    .shift(select),
    .out(rotator_out_wire)
);

counter counter_inst (
    .clk(clk),
    .reset(reset),
    .out(counter_out_wire)
);

always @(*) begin
    case (select)
        2'b00: begin
            rotator_out = rotator_out_wire;
            counter_out = 4'b0;
        end
        2'b01: begin
            rotator_out = 100'b0;
            counter_out = counter_out_wire;
        end
        default: begin
            rotator_out = 100'b0;
            counter_out = 4'b0;
        end
    endcase
end

endmodule

module top_module ( 
    input clk,                  // System clock
    input reset,                // Synchronous active-high reset
    input [1:0] select,         // Select input to choose between rotator and counter
    input [99:0] data,          // 100-bit input for the rotator
    output [3:0] counter_out,   // 4-bit output from the counter
    output [99:0] rotator_out   // 100-bit output from the rotator
);

wire [99:0] rotator_out_wire;      // Wire to hold rotator output
wire [3:0] counter_out_wire;       // Wire to hold counter output

control_logic control_inst (
    .select(select),
    .rotator_data(data),
    .counter_data(counter_out_wire),
    .rotator_out(rotator_out_wire),
    .counter_out(counter_out_wire)
);

endmodule

module Add_Subtract_32bit(
  input [31:0] A,
  input [31:0] B,
  input Subtract,
  input CLK,
  input RST,
  output reg [31:0] Result,
  output reg Overflow
);

  always @(posedge CLK, negedge RST) begin
    if (!RST) begin
      Result <= 0;
      Overflow <= 0;
    end
    else begin
      if (Subtract) begin
        Result <= A - B;
        if (A < B) begin
          Overflow <= 1;
        end
        else begin
          Overflow <= 0;
        end
      end
      else begin
        Result <= A + B;
        if (Result < A || Result < B) begin
          Overflow <= 1;
        end
        else begin
          Overflow <= 0;
        end
      end
    end
  end

endmodule

A multiplier circuit is a type of digital circuit that can perform multiplication operation on two numbers. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: two n-bit numbers (A and B), a control signal (ctrl)
Outputs: one 2n-bit number (P)

The module should also have the following parameters:

n: the number of bits in the input numbers (A and B)

Your module should implement the following functionality:

If the control signal is 0, the circuit should perform unsigned multiplication on the input numbers.
If the control signal is 1, the circuit should perform signed multiplication on the input numbers.
The output signal should be a 2n-bit number that represents the result of the multiplication operation.
To implement the multiplier circuit, you should use Verilog code to perform multiplication operation on the input numbers based on the control signal. 
For unsigned multiplication, you can use a simple shift and add algorithm. For signed multiplication, you can use the Booth's algorithm.
Finally, you should concatenate the result of the multiplication operation to form the 2n-bit output signal.
Response:
module multiplier (
  input [n-1:0] A,
  input [n-1:0] B,
  input ctrl,
  output reg [2*n-1:0] P
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits in the input numbers

always @(*) begin
  if (ctrl == 0) begin // unsigned multiplication
    P = {2*n{1'b0}}; // initialize P to 0
    for (i = 0; i < n; i = i + 1) begin
      if (B[i] == 1) begin
        P = P + (A << i);
      end
    end
  end
  else begin // signed multiplication
    P = {2*n{1'b0}}; // initialize P to 0
    if (A[n-1] == 1) begin // sign extend A
      A = {{n{1'b1}}, A};
    end
    if (B[n-1] == 1) begin // sign extend B
      B = {{n{1'b1}}, B};
    end
    for (i = 0; i < n; i = i + 1) begin
      if (B[i] == 1) begin
        P = P + (A << i);
      end
    end
    // Booth's algorithm for signed multiplication
    for (i = 0; i < n-1; i = i + 1) begin
      if (B[i] == 1 && B[i+1] == 0) begin // 01 pattern
        P = P - (A << (i+1));
      end
      else if (B[i] == 0 && B[i+1] == 1) begin // 10 pattern
        P = P + (A << (i+1));
      end
    end
  end
end

endmodule

- `AW`: address bus width (default: clog2(DEPTH))

The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

- `en`: memory access signal
- `we`: write enable global signal
- `wem`: write enable vector
- `addr`: address

- `dout`: data output

The module should also have the following power/repair inputs:

- `vss`: common ground
- `vdd`: periphery power rail
- `vddm`: sram array power rail
- `shutdown`: shutdown signal from always-on domain
- `memconfig`: generic memory config
- `memrepair`: repair vector

Finally, the module should also have the following BIST inputs:

- `bist_en`: BIST enable
- `bist_we`: write enable global signal
- `bist_wem`: write enable vector
- `bist_addr`: address
- `bist_din`: data input

module single_port_memory #(
  parameter DW = 104,          // memory width
  parameter DEPTH = 32,        // memory depth
  parameter MCW = 8,           // repair/config width
  parameter AW = $clog2(DEPTH) // address bus width
) (
  input clk,                   // clock
  input en,                    // memory access
  input we,                    // write enable global signal
  input [DW-1:0] wem,          // write enable vector
  input [AW-1:0] addr,         // address
  input [DW-1:0] din,          // data input
  output [DW-1:0] dout,        // data output
  input vss,                   // common ground
  input vdd,                   // periphery power rail
  input vddm,                  // sram array power rail
  input shutdown,              // shutdown signal from always-on domain
  input [MCW-1:0] memconfig,   // generic memory config
  input [MCW-1:0] memrepair,   // repair vector
  input bist_en,               // bist enable
  input bist_we,               // bist write enable global signal
  input [DW-1:0] bist_wem,     // bist write enable vector
  input [AW-1:0] bist_addr,    // bist address
  input [DW-1:0] bist_din      // bist data input
);

  // Declare the memory array
  reg [DW-1:0] memory [0:DEPTH-1];

  // Write to the memory array when we have both the enable and write signals high
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (en && we) begin
      if (wem == {DW{1'b1}}) begin
        memory[addr] <= din;
      end else begin
        memory[addr] <= {memory[addr][DW-1:0] & ~wem, din};
      end
    end
  end

  // Read from the memory array when we have the enable signal high
  always @(*) begin
    if (en) begin
      dout <= memory[addr];
    end
  end

endmodule

    input a, b, // Two bits to be added
    input select, // Select input to choose between half adder module and functional module
    output [1:0] sum // 2-bit output from the active module
);

    wire [1:0] sum_functional; // Declare wire for sum output from functional module

    functional_module fm(sum_half_adder, cout, sum_functional); // Instantiate functional module

);
    assign sum = a ^ b; // XOR gate for sum output
    assign cout = a & b; // AND gate for carry-out output
endmodule

module functional_module(
    input sum_half_adder, cout_half_adder,
    output [1:0] sum // 2-bit sum output
);
    wire carry_in;
    assign carry_in = cout_half_adder; // Connect carry-out from half adder module to carry-in of full adder module
    
    full_adder fa(sum_half_adder, {1'b0, carry_in}, sum); // Instantiate full adder module
endmodule

module full_adder(
    input a, b, cin,
    output cout, sum // Carry-out and sum outputs
);
    wire s1, c1, c2;
    
    assign s1 = a ^ b; // XOR gate for first stage sum output
    assign c1 = a & b; // AND gate for first stage carry-out output
    assign sum = s1 ^ cin; // XOR gate for final sum output
    assign c2 = s1 & cin; // AND gate for final carry-out output
    
    assign cout = c1 | c2; // OR gate for final carry-out output
endmodule

- a write enable signal (write_en)
- a reset signal (reset)

Outputs: 
- a set of m output signals (data_out)

The module should also have the following parameters:

- n: the number of bits in each data input signal.
- m: the number of bits in each data output signal.
- k: the number of registers in the register file.

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- The circuit should have k registers, each of which is n bits wide.
- The circuit should have a read operation and a write operation.
- The read operation should read the contents of a selected register and output the data on the data bus.
- The write operation should write the data on the data input signals to a selected register when the write enable signal is high.
- The reset signal should reset all the registers to zero.

To implement the register file, you should use Verilog code to define the registers as arrays and implement the read and write operations using multiplexers and tri-state buffers. 
You should also use the reset signal to clear all the registers to zero.

module register_file (
  input [n-1:0] data_in,
  input [k-1:0] reg_select,
  input write_en,
  input reset,
  output [m-1:0] data_out
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits in each data input signal
parameter m = 8; // number of bits in each data output signal
parameter k = 8; // number of registers in the register file

reg [n-1:0] registers [0:k-1]; // array of k registers, each n bits wide

assign data_out = (reg_select < k) ? registers[reg_select] : 0; // read operation using a multiplexer

always @ (posedge clk) begin // write operation using a tri-state buffer
  if (write_en) begin
    registers[reg_select] <= data_in;
  end
end

always @ (posedge clk) begin // reset operation
  if (reset) begin
    for (i = 0; i < k; i = i + 1) begin
      registers[i] <= 0;
    end
  end
end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a hysteresis comparator. 
A hysteresis comparator is a type of comparator that includes positive feedback, which causes the output to switch at different input levels depending on whether the input is increasing or decreasing. 
This means that the output will switch at a different threshold when the input is rising compared to when it is falling. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a single input signal (in)
Outputs: a single output signal (out)
The module should also have the following parameters:

vth1: the upper threshold voltage of the comparator
vth2: the lower threshold voltage of the comparator
vref: the reference voltage for the comparator
Your module should implement the following functionality:

When the input signal is greater than or equal to vth1, the output signal should be high.
When the input signal is less than or equal to vth2, the output signal should be low.
When the input signal is between vth1 and vth2, the output signal should maintain its current state.
The hysteresis of the comparator should be determined by the difference between vth1 and vth2.
To implement the hysteresis comparator, you should use Verilog code to compare the input signal to the threshold voltages and output the appropriate signal. 
You should also use positive feedback to ensure that the output switches at different thresholds depending on the direction of the input signal.

module hysteresis_comp (
  input in,
  output out
);

parameter vth1 = 1.5; // upper threshold voltage
parameter vth2 = 1.0; // lower threshold voltage
parameter vref = 0.5; // reference voltage

reg out_reg; // output register for positive feedback

always @ (in or out_reg) begin
  if (in >= vth1) begin
    out_reg <= 1'b1;
  end else if (in <= vth2) begin
    out_reg <= 1'b0;
  end else begin
    out_reg <= out_reg; // maintain current state
  end
end

assign out = out_reg;

endmodule

I2C is a communication protocol commonly used in integrated circuits for short-distance, intra-board communication. 
The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- clk: the clock signal
- rst: the reset signal
- sda: the data signal
- scl: the clock signal
Outputs: 
- ack: the acknowledge signal

The I2C state machine should have the following states:
- IDLE: waiting for start condition
- ADDR: waiting for address byte
- DATA: waiting for data byte
- STOP: waiting for stop condition
- ERROR: error state

The module should implement the following functionality:
- The state machine should start in the IDLE state.
- When a start condition is detected on the bus, the state machine should transition to the ADDR state.
- In the ADDR state, the state machine should wait for an address byte on the bus. If the address byte matches the module's address, the state machine should transition to the DATA state. Otherwise, it should transition to the ERROR state.
- In the DATA state, the state machine should wait for data bytes on the bus. It should acknowledge each byte and store the data in a buffer. When all data bytes have been received, the state machine should transition to the STOP state.
- In the STOP state, the state machine should wait for a stop condition on the bus. Once the stop condition is detected, the state machine should reset and return to the IDLE state.
- If any errors are detected during the communication, the state machine should transition to the ERROR state.

To implement the I2C state machine, you should use Verilog code to define the state transitions and the behavior of the module in each state. You should also use the input signals to detect start, stop, address, and data bytes on the bus. Finally, you should use the output signal to acknowledge data bytes and indicate errors.

module i2c_state_machine (
  input clk,
  input rst,
  input sda,
  input scl,
  output reg ack
);

parameter ADDR_WIDTH = 7; // address width in bits

reg [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] addr; // address register
reg [7:0] data; // data buffer
reg [2:0] state; // state register

// State encoding
localparam IDLE = 3'b000,
           ADDR = 3'b001,
           DATA = 3'b010,
           STOP = 3'b011,
           ERROR = 3'b100;

always @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
  if (rst) begin
    state <= IDLE;
    ack <= 0;
  end else begin
    case (state)
      IDLE: begin
        if (sda == 0 && scl == 1) // start condition
          state <= ADDR;
      end
      ADDR: begin
        if (scl == 1) begin
          addr <= {addr[ADDR_WIDTH-2:0], sda};
          if (addr == MY_ADDR) // assuming MY_ADDR is the module's address
            state <= DATA;
          else
            state <= ERROR;
        end
      end
      DATA: begin
        if (scl == 1) begin
          data <= {data[6:0], sda};
          ack <= 1;
        end else begin
          ack <= 0;
          state <= STOP;
        end
      end
      STOP: begin
        if (sda == 1 && scl == 1) // stop condition
          state <= IDLE;
      end
      ERROR: begin
        // handle error state if needed
      end
      default: begin
        state <= IDLE;
      end
    endcase
  end
end

endmodule

  input [WIDTH-1:0] din2,

You should then use this counter to determine when to update the output signal based on the value of t.

module glitch_filter (
  input clk,
  input in,
  output out
);

  parameter t = 10; // minimum duration of a valid signal (in clock cycles)
  
  reg [3:0] count = 0; // counter to count clock cycles
  
  reg prev_in = 0; // previous value of input signal
  
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (in != prev_in) begin // input signal has changed
      count <= 0; // reset counter
    end else begin // input signal has not changed
      if (count < t) begin // wait for t clock cycles
        count <= count + 1;
      end else begin // t clock cycles have passed
        out <= in; // update output signal
      end
    end
    prev_in <= in; // update previous value of input signal
  end
  
endmodule

An ADC is a type of circuit that converts an analog signal into a digital signal. The input analog signal can be any voltage within a certain range, and the output digital signal is a binary representation of the input voltage.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: an analog input signal (analog_in)
Outputs: an 8-bit digital output signal (digital_out)
The module should also have the following parameters:

vref: the reference voltage used for the ADC (e.g., 5V)
res: the resolution of the ADC (e.g., 8 bits)

The output digital value should be an 8-bit binary representation of the analog signal, with the most significant bit (MSB) being the sign bit and the remaining bits representing the magnitude of the signal.

You should then use this algorithm to convert the analog signal into an 8-bit binary representation.
Finally, you should output the digital value on the digital_out port.

module ADC (
  input analog_in,
  output reg [7:0] digital_out
);

parameter vref = 5; // reference voltage
parameter res = 8; // resolution of ADC (in bits)

reg [7:0] count;

always @ (posedge analog_in) begin
  if (analog_in > (vref/2)) begin
    count <= {1, {res-1{1'b1}}}; // positive voltage
  end else begin
    count <= {1'b0, {res-1{1'b0}}}; // negative voltage
  end
end

assign digital_out = count;

endmodule

module shift_register (
    input [3:0] D, // Data input
    input LD, // Load input
    input CLK, // Clock input
    input CLR, // Clear input
    output reg [3:0] Q // Data output
);

    always @(posedge CLK, posedge CLR) begin
        if (CLR) begin
            Q <= 4'b0000; // Reset to all zeros
        end else if (LD) begin
            Q <= D; // Load data into register
        end else begin
            Q <= {Q[2:0], Q[3]}; // Shift data left
        end
    end

endmodule

module adder (
    input [3:0] A, B,
    output [3:0] sum
);

    assign sum = A + B;

endmodule

module top_module (
    input [3:0] D1, D2,
    input LD1, LD2, CLK, CLR,
    output reg [3:0] Q1, Q2,
    output [3:0] sum
);

    shift_register sr1 (
        .D(D1),
        .LD(LD1),
        .CLK(CLK),
        .CLR(CLR),
        .Q(Q1)
    );

    shift_register sr2 (
        .D(Q1),
        .LD(LD2),
        .CLK(CLK),
        .CLR(CLR),
        .Q(Q2)
    );

    adder add (
        .A(Q1),
        .B(Q2),
        .sum(sum)
    );

endmodule

The calculator should have two input ports, `op1` and `op2`, which are 4-bit signed integers. The calculator should also have an input port, `op`, which is a 2-bit value representing the operation to be performed. The output of the calculator should be a 4-bit signed integer, `result`.

The possible values for `op` are as follows:
- `2'b00`: Addition
- `2'b01`: Subtraction
- `2'b10`: Multiplication
- `2'b11`: Division

For addition and subtraction, the output should be the result of adding or subtracting `op1` and `op2`. For multiplication and division, the output should be the result of multiplying or dividing `op1` and `op2`, respectively. If the result of the division operation is not an integer, it should be rounded towards zero.

module calculator(
    input signed [3:0] op1,
    input signed [3:0] op2,
    input [1:0] op,
    output reg signed [3:0] result
);

always @(*)
    case(op)
        2'b00: result = op1 + op2; // Addition
        2'b01: result = op1 - op2; // Subtraction
        2'b10: result = op1 * op2; // Multiplication
        2'b11: begin                // Division
                    if(op2 == 0) begin
                        result = 4'bX; // Indeterminate result
                    end
                    else if((op1 == -8) && (op2 == -1)) begin
                        result = 4'bX; // Overflow condition
                    end
                    else begin
                        result = op1 / op2; // Integer division
                    end
               end
    endcase

endmodule

module readdata_module (

The `DE` input is an enable signal that determines whether the flip-flop is enabled or disabled. When `DE` is low, the flip-flop should hold its current state, regardless of any changes in the `D` input. When `DE` is high, the flip-flop should update its output to match the `D` input on the next rising edge of `CLK`. 

The `VPWR` and `VGND` inputs are power and ground respectively.

module my_flip_flop (
    output Q   ,
    input  CLK ,
    input  D   ,
    input  DE  ,
    input  VPWR,
    input  VGND
);

    reg Q;

    always @(posedge CLK) begin
        if (DE) begin
            Q <= D;
        end
    end

endmodule

module memory_block (
  input wr_clk, // Write clock
  input rd_clk, // Read clock
  input [0:0] E, // Enable signal
  input [63:0] din, // Data input
  output [63:0] dout // Data output
);

    if (E) begin // If enable signal is high
      mem[1] <= din[63:32]; // Write upper 32 bits to mem[1]

  end

    dout <= {mem[1], mem[0]}; // Read data from memory block
  end

endmodule

module shift_register (
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input data_in,
    input shift_in,
    output reg [7:0] data_out
);

            data_out <= 8'h00;

            if (shift_in) begin

    input enable,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

    end else if (enable) begin

end

- `byteena_b`: A signal that is always set to `cst_std_logic_vector_type_one[0]`.

- When `tagram_wren_b` is low, read the data from the TAG RAM at the address specified by `tagram_address_b` and output it on `tagram_q_b`.

module tag_ram (
    input [7:0] tagram_data_b,
    input tagram_wren_b,
    input [7:0] tagram_address_b,
    input cst_one,
    input cst_zero,
    input [0:0] cst_std_logic_vector_type_one,
    output [7:0] tagram_q_b
);

reg [7:0] tag_ram_array [255:0]; // 256 x 8-bit RAM array

reg [7:0] q_a; // internal signal for reading data from RAM

// always block for writing to RAM
always @ (posedge cst_one) begin
    if (tagram_wren_b) begin
        tag_ram_array[tagram_address_b] <= tagram_data_b;
    end
end

// always block for reading from RAM
always @ (posedge cst_one) begin
    if (!tagram_wren_b) begin
        q_a <= tag_ram_array[tagram_address_b];
    end
end

assign tagram_q_b = q_a; // output the read data

endmodule

module RAM (
  input clk,
  input en,
  input we,
  input [log2(depth)-1:0] addr,
  input [width-1:0] data_in,
  output [width-1:0] data_out
);

parameter width = 8; // width of the data bus
parameter depth = 256; // depth of the memory

reg [width-1:0] memory [0:depth-1]; // array of registers to store data

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (en) begin // check if RAM block is active
    if (we) begin // check if write enable signal is high
      memory[addr] <= data_in; // write data to selected memory location
    end
    data_out <= memory[addr]; // read data from selected memory location
  end
end

endmodule

You are tasked with designing a Verilog module that implements a simple 2-to-1 multiplexer. The module should have two input ports (`in0` and `in1`) and one output port (`out`).
```
module mux_2to1(
    input in0,
    input in1,
    input sel,
    output reg out
);
```

Ensure that all inputs and outputs are of the correct data type, and that the module is synthesizable.
Response:
module mux_2to1(
    input in0,
    input in1,
    input sel,
    output reg out
);

always @ (sel, in0, in1) begin
    if (sel) begin
        out <= in1;
    end else begin
        out <= in0;
    end
end

endmodule

module binary_counter (
    input clk,
    input rst,
    input en,
    output reg [3:0] count
);

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst) begin
        if (!rst) begin
            count <= 4'b0000;
        end else if (en) begin
            count <= count + 1;
        end
    end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a bus hold block.
A bus hold block is a type of digital circuit that is used to avoid glitches in a bus signal caused by the changing state of the signal's inputs.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a bus signal (bus_in), a clock signal (clk), a reset signal (reset)
Outputs: a bus signal (bus_out)
The module should also have the following parameters:

n: the number of bits in the bus signal
Your module should implement the following functionality:

The circuit should hold the value of the bus signal when the clock signal is low.
When the clock signal goes high, the circuit should latch the value of the bus signal and hold it until the clock signal goes low again.
The circuit should also have a reset input that sets the output bus signal to 0 when it is active.
To implement the bus hold block, you should use Verilog code to define a D flip-flop that is triggered by the rising edge of the clock signal.
The input to the flip-flop should be the bus signal, and the output should be the output bus signal.
You should also use a multiplexer to select between the input bus signal and the output bus signal based on the value of the reset signal.
Finally, you should use an always block to implement the bus hold functionality, which should hold the output bus signal when the clock signal is low and latch the input bus signal when the clock signal is high.
Response:
module bus_hold (
  input [n-1:0] bus_in,
  input clk,
  input reset,
  output [n-1:0] bus_out
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits in the bus signal

reg [n-1:0] bus_hold_reg; // register to hold the bus signal

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) begin
    bus_hold_reg <= 0;
  end else begin
    bus_hold_reg <= bus_in;
  end
end

assign bus_out = reset ? 0 : bus_hold_reg;

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a multiplier circuit for unsigned and signed inputs. The multiplier circuit should be able to multiply two n-bit unsigned or signed binary numbers and produce a 2n-bit result. The multiplier should use a combinational logic implementation.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: two n-bit binary numbers (A and B) and a control signal (ctrl)
Outputs: a 2n-bit binary number (result)

Your module should implement the following functionality:

If the control signal (ctrl) is 0, the module should multiply two unsigned binary numbers (A and B) and produce an unsigned 2n-bit result.
If the control signal (ctrl) is 1, the module should multiply two signed binary numbers (A and B) and produce a signed 2n-bit result.
To implement the multiplier, you should use Verilog code to define the multiplication algorithm for unsigned and signed inputs as Boolean functions. You should then use these functions to implement the combinational logic that performs the multiplication based on the control signal.

For unsigned multiplication, you can use a simple algorithm that involves adding shifted values of the first number (A) based on the bits of the second number (B).

For signed multiplication, you can use the Booth's algorithm that reduces the number of partial products needed to be added. The algorithm works by examining adjacent pairs of bits in B and shifting the multiplicand A by different amounts depending on the bit pair (00, 01, 10). Booth's algorithm is more efficient than the simple unsigned multiplication for signed numbers.
Response:
module multiplier (
  input [n-1:0] A,
  input [n-1:0] B,
  input ctrl,
  output reg [2*n-1:0] result
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits for A and B

// Unsigned multiplication
always @(*) begin
  if(ctrl == 0) begin
    result = {2*n{1'b0}}; // initialize result to 0
    for (i = 0; i < n; i = i+1) begin
      if (B[i] == 1'b1) begin
        result = result + (A << i);
      end
    end
  end
  // Signed multiplication
  else begin
    result = {2*n{1'b0}}; // initialize result to 0
    A_signed = $signed(A);
    B_signed = $signed(B);
    for (i = 0; i < n; i = i+1) begin
      if (B[i] == 1'b1) begin
        if (i == 0) begin
          result = result + A_signed;
        end
        else if (B[i-1] == 1'b0) begin
          result = result + (A_signed << i);
        end
        else begin
          result = result + (A_signed << i) - A_signed;
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

endmodule

The opcode input should be interpreted as follows:
- 00: addition (A + B)
- 01: subtraction (A - B)
- 10: multiplication (A * B)
- 11: division (A / B)

The calculator should only perform the operation when the enable signal is high (en = 1). If the enable signal is low (en = 0), the calculator should output 0.

Assume that all inputs and outputs are unsigned. You may assume that the inputs will always be valid 8-bit unsigned integers and that division by zero will never occur.

module calculator(
    input [7:0] A,
    input [7:0] B,
    input [1:0] opcode,
    input en,
    output reg [7:0] R
);

always @(*) begin
    if (en == 1) begin
        case(opcode)
            2'b00: R = A + B; // addition
            2'b01: R = A - B; // subtraction
            2'b10: R = A * B; // multiplication
            2'b11: R = A / B; // division
        endcase
    end else begin
        R = 8'b0;
    end
end

endmodule

module counter(
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input enable,
  output reg [3:0] count
);

    end else if (enable) begin

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a delay block. 
A delay block is a type of digital circuit that introduces a delay in the input signal before passing it to the output. 
This can be useful in certain applications where a delay is required for synchronization or timing purposes. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a single input signal (in)
Outputs: a single output signal (out)
The module should also have the following parameter:

delay: the amount of delay to introduce (in time units)
Your module should implement the following functionality:

The output signal should be a delayed version of the input signal, where the delay is equal to the value of the delay parameter.
To implement the delay block, you should use Verilog code to create a shift register that is long enough to store the input signal for the desired delay period. 
You should then use the shift register to introduce the delay and connect the delayed signal to the output.
Note that the delay should be implemented using non-blocking assignments to ensure that the delayed signal is computed correctly.
Response:
module delay_block (
  input in,
  output out
);

parameter delay = 10; // delay in time units

reg [delay-1:0] shift_reg; // shift register to store input signal

always @(posedge clk) begin
  shift_reg <= {in, shift_reg[delay-2:0]}; // shift input signal into shift register
end

assign out = shift_reg[delay-1]; // output delayed signal

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Create a module that implements a 4-bit shift register with parallel load. The module should have four inputs: a 4-bit data input (din), a clock input (clk), a parallel load input (load), and a reset input (reset). The module should have one output, a 4-bit shift register output (sro). The module should shift the data input by one bit position on each rising clock edge. If the parallel load input is asserted, the module should load the data input into the shift register on the next rising clock edge. If the reset input is asserted, the module should set the shift register output to 0.
Response:
module shift_register (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input load,
  input [3:0] din,
  output reg [3:0] sro
);

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if(reset) begin
      sro <= 4'b0000;
    end else if(load) begin
      sro <= din;
    end else begin
      sro <= {sro[2:0], din[3]};
    end
  end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a light control block for ambient light sensing and dimming.
The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- ambient light sensor (als): a 12-bit signal that represents the ambient light level
- desired light level (dll): a 12-bit signal that represents the desired light level
- enable signal (en): a single bit signal that enables the module

Outputs:
- dimming signal (dim): a 8-bit signal that controls the brightness of the light

The module should implement the following functionality:
- When the enable signal is high, the module should compare the ambient light level to the desired light level to determine the dimming level.
- The dimming level should be calculated as follows:
  - If the ambient light level is less than or equal to the desired light level, the dimming level should be set to 0.
  - Otherwise, the dimming level should be calculated as (ambient light level - desired light level) / 16.
- The dimming level should be clamped to the range of 0 to 255.
- When the enable signal is low, the dimming level should be set to 0.

To implement the light control block, you should use Verilog code to define the calculations for the dimming level based on the input signals. 
You should also define the enable signal and use it to control the output of the dimming signal.
Response:
module light_control (
  input [11:0] als,
  input [11:0] dll,
  input en,
  output reg [7:0] dim
);

  always @(*) begin
    if (en) begin
      if (als <= dll) begin
        dim <= 8'b00000000;
      end else begin
        dim <= ((als - dll) >> 4) > 8'b11111111 ? 8'b11111111 : ((als - dll) >> 4);
      end
    end else begin
      dim <= 8'b00000000;
    end
  end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a one-shot pulse generator, also known as a monostable multivibrator. 
A one-shot pulse generator produces a single pulse output in response to a trigger input. The pulse width of the output can be adjusted by changing the values of the components in the circuit.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- trigger: a single-bit input signal that triggers the pulse generation
- pulse_width: a parameter that sets the width of the output pulse (in time units)

Outputs: 
- pulse: a single-bit output signal that generates the pulse

Your module should implement the following functionality:
- When the trigger input goes high, the pulse output should go high and stay high for the duration of the pulse width parameter.
- After the pulse width has elapsed, the pulse output should go low again.

To implement the one-shot pulse generator, you should use Verilog code to define a counter that counts up to the pulse width parameter and generates a pulse when it reaches the end. 
You should then use this counter in conjunction with the trigger input to generate the output pulse. 
Finally, you should use the pulse output to drive any downstream logic that requires a single pulse input.
Response:
module one_shot (
  input trigger,
  output pulse
);

  parameter pulse_width = 10; // pulse width in time units
  
  reg [7:0] count; // 8-bit counter to count up to pulse_width
  
  always @(posedge trigger) begin
    count <= 0; // reset counter on trigger
    pulse <= 1; // set pulse high on trigger
  end
  
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (count < pulse_width) begin
      count <= count + 1; // increment counter
    end else begin
      pulse <= 0; // set pulse low after pulse_width
    end
  end
  
endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Create a Verilog module that implements a 3-bit up/down counter. The counter should increment when the up signal is asserted and decrement when the down signal is asserted. The counter should wrap around to zero when it reaches its maximum value or minimum value. Additionally, the module should have a reset input that sets the counter to zero when asserted.
Response:
module up_down_counter (
  input clk,
  input reset,
  input up,
  input down,
  output reg [2:0] count
);

  always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
    if (reset) begin
      count <= 3'b0;
    end else if (up) begin
      if (count == 3'b111) begin
        count <= 3'b0;
      end else begin
        count <= count + 1;
      end
    end else if (down) begin
      if (count == 3'b000) begin
        count <= 3'b111;
      end else begin
        count <= count - 1;
      end
    end
  end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements an up/down binary counter. 
A binary counter is a digital circuit that counts in binary from 0 to 2^n-1, where n is the number of bits in the counter. 
An up/down binary counter can count up or down, depending on the value of a control signal.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a clock signal (clk), a reset signal (rst), an enable signal (en), a direction signal (dir), and a count signal (count_in)
Outputs: a count signal (count_out)

The module should also have the following parameters:

n: the number of bits in the counter

Your module should implement the following functionality:

The counter should count in binary from 0 to 2^n-1 when the direction signal (dir) is 1 (i.e., counting up).
The counter should count in binary from 2^n-1 to 0 when the direction signal (dir) is 0 (i.e., counting down).
The counter should be reset to 0 when the reset signal (rst) is asserted.
The counter should only count when the enable signal (en) is asserted.
The count signal (count_in) should be used as the initial value of the counter.

To implement the up/down binary counter, you should use Verilog code to define the behavior of the counter based on the value of the direction signal. 
You should use a register to store the current count value, and you should use combinational logic to compute the next count value based on the current count value and the direction signal. 
You should also use combinational logic to determine when the counter should be reset to 0 or when it should continue counting. 
Finally, you should use the clock signal to update the count register with the next count value.

module up_down_counter (
  input clk,
  input rst,
  input en,
  input dir,
  input [n-1:0] count_in,
  output reg [n-1:0] count_out
);

parameter n = 4; // number of bits in the counter

reg [n-1:0] count_reg;

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin
    count_reg <= 0;
  end else if (en) begin
    if (dir) begin // counting up
      if (count_reg == 2**n-1) begin
        count_reg <= 0;
      end else begin
        count_reg <= count_reg + 1;
      end
    end else begin // counting down
      if (count_reg == 0) begin
        count_reg <= 2**n-1;
      end else begin
        count_reg <= count_reg - 1;
      end
    end
  end
end

assign count_out = (en) ? count_reg : count_in;

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a phase-locked loop (PLL). 
A PLL is a circuit that generates an output signal with a frequency that is locked to the frequency of an input signal. 
PLLs are widely used in communication systems, where they are used to generate stable clock signals for digital circuits.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Your module should also have the following parameters:

- N: the multiplication factor of the PLL
- M: the division factor of the PLL

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- The PLL should multiply the frequency of the input clock signal by N and divide it by M to generate an output clock signal with a frequency of F.
- The PLL should use a phase-frequency detector (PFD) to compare the phase and frequency of the input and output clock signals.
- The PLL should use a charge pump to generate a control voltage based on the output of the PFD.
- The PLL should use a loop filter to filter the control voltage and generate a stable voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) frequency.
- The PLL should use a frequency divider to divide the VCO frequency by M to generate the output clock signal.

To implement the PLL, you should use Verilog code to define the PFD, charge pump, loop filter, and frequency divider as separate modules. 
You should then use these modules to connect the inputs and outputs of the PLL module.
You should also use Verilog code to define the state machine that controls the operation of the PLL.

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a cache memory block. 
A cache memory block is a type of computer memory that is used to temporarily store frequently used data. 
The inputs to the circuit are the address of the data that needs to be accessed, and the output is the data stored at that address.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- a set of n address signals (addr1, addr2, ..., addrn)
- a set of m write data signals (data_in1, data_in2, ..., data_inm)
- a write enable signal (we)
- a read enable signal (re)

Outputs: 
- a set of m read data signals (data_out1, data_out2, ..., data_outm)

The module should also have the following parameters:
- n: the number of address signals
- m: the number of data signals
- b: the number of data blocks in the cache memory
- w: the number of words in each data block

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- The circuit should have b data blocks, each of which contains w words.
- The circuit should be able to read and write data to and from the cache memory.
- When a read or write operation is performed, the circuit should use the address signals to determine which data block to access, and which word within the data block to access.
- When a write operation is performed, the circuit should use the write enable signal to determine whether to write the data to the cache memory.
- When a read operation is performed, the circuit should use the read enable signal to determine whether to output the data stored at the specified address.

To implement the cache memory block, you should use Verilog code to define the data blocks and the word within each data block. 
You should then use these blocks to connect the inputs to the cache memory and the cache memory to the output signals.
Finally, you should use the read and write enable signals to control the read and write operations.
Response:
module cache_memory_block (
  input [n-1:0] addr,
  input [m-1:0] data_in,
  input we,
  input re,
  output [m-1:0] data_out
);

parameter n = 8; // number of address signals
parameter m = 32; // number of data signals
parameter b = 16; // number of data blocks
parameter w = 8; // number of words in each data block

reg [m-1:0] cache_mem [b-1:0][w-1:0]; // data blocks in the cache memory

integer i, j; // loop variables

always @(*) begin
  if (we) begin // write operation
    for (i = 0; i < b; i = i + 1) begin
      if (addr >= i*w && addr < (i+1)*w) begin // check which data block to access
        cache_mem[i][addr-i*w] = data_in; // write data to the cache memory
      end
    end
  end
  
  if (re) begin // read operation
    for (i = 0; i < b; i = i + 1) begin
      if (addr >= i*w && addr < (i+1)*w) begin // check which data block to access
        data_out = cache_mem[i][addr-i*w]; // output data stored at the specified address
      end
    end
  end
end

endmodule

This is important because the initial state of the circuit is unknown when power is first applied, and it may cause unpredictable behavior. 
The reset signal is used to initialize the circuit to a known state.

After a delay of "delay" seconds, the reset signal should be high.
To implement the POR circuit, you should use Verilog code to define the delay as a time parameter. 
You should then use an initial block to set the reset signal to low when power is first applied. 
Finally, you should use a delay block to generate the reset signal after the specified delay.

module POR (
  input VDD,
  output RST
);

parameter delay = 1; // delay time in seconds

reg RST_reg; // internal register to hold reset signal

initial begin
  RST_reg = 0; // set reset signal to low when power is first applied
end

always @(VDD) begin
  if (VDD == 1'b1) begin
    #(delay * 1_000_000) RST_reg = 1; // generate reset signal after delay
  end
end

assign RST = RST_reg; // assign internal register to output

endmodule

You are tasked with implementing a clock module in Verilog. The module should take in an input clock signal, `CLK_IN1`, and output three clock signals, `CLK_OUT1`, `CLK_OUT2`, and `CLK_OUT3`, all of which have a frequency of 83 MHz. Additionally, the module should have a `RESET` input and a `LOCKED` output.

To accomplish this, you will need to use the `MMCM_ADV` primitive to generate the output clocks. The `MMCM_ADV` primitive has a number of inputs and outputs, including `CLKFBOUT`, which is used as feedback to adjust the output frequency, and `CLKOUT0`, `CLKOUT1`, and `CLKOUT2`, which are the output clock signals. You will also need to use input buffering and output buffering primitives, `IBUFG` and `BUFG`, respectively, to properly buffer the input and output signals.

Your implementation should be contained within a single Verilog module that is no more than 200 lines of code.

module clock_module
(
  input         CLK_IN1,
  output        CLK_OUT1,
  output        CLK_OUT2,
  output        CLK_OUT3,
  input         RESET,
  output        LOCKED
);

  // Input buffering
  //------------------------------------
  IBUFG clkin1_buf
   (.O (clkin1),
    .I (CLK_IN1));

  // Clocking primitive
  //------------------------------------
  wire        clkfbout;
  wire        clkfbout_buf;
  wire        clkout0;
  wire        clkout1;
  wire        clkout2;
  wire        locked;

  MMCM_ADV
  #(.BANDWIDTH            ("OPTIMIZED"),
    .CLKOUT4_CASCADE      ("FALSE"),
    .CLOCK_HOLD           ("FALSE"),
    .COMPENSATION         ("ZHOLD"),
    .STARTUP_WAIT         ("FALSE"),
    .DIVCLK_DIVIDE        (1),
    .CLKFBOUT_MULT_F      (40.000),
    .CLKFBOUT_PHASE       (0.000),
    .CLKFBOUT_USE_FINE_PS ("FALSE"),
    .CLKOUT0_DIVIDE_F     (6.000),
    .CLKOUT0_PHASE        (0.000),
    .CLKOUT0_DUTY_CYCLE   (0.500),
    .CLKOUT0_USE_FINE_PS  ("FALSE"),
    .CLKOUT1_DIVIDE       (12),
    .CLKOUT1_PHASE        (0.000),
    .CLKOUT1_DUTY_CYCLE   (0.500),
    .CLKOUT1_USE_FINE_PS  ("FALSE"),
    .CLKOUT2_DIVIDE       (12),
    .CLKOUT2_PHASE        (180.000),
    .CLKOUT2_DUTY_CYCLE   (0.500),
    .CLKOUT2_USE_FINE_PS  ("FALSE"),
    .CLKIN1_PERIOD        (40.000),
    .REF_JITTER1          (0.010))
  mmcm_adv_inst
    // Output clocks
   (.CLKFBOUT            (clkfbout),
    .CLKFBOUTB           (),
    .CLKOUT0             (clkout0),
    .CLKOUT0B            (),
    .CLKOUT1             (clkout1),
    .CLKOUT1B            (),
    .CLKOUT2             (clkout2),
    .CLKOUT2B            (),
     // Input clock control
    .CLKFBIN             (clkfbout_buf),
    .CLKIN1              (clkin1),
    .CLKIN2              (),
     // Tied to always select the primary input clock
    .CLKINSEL            (1'b1),
    // Ports for dynamic reconfiguration
    .DADDR               (),
    .DCLK                (),
    .DEN                 (),
    .DI                  (),
    .DO                  (),
    .DRDY                (),
    .DWE                 (),
    // Ports for dynamic phase shift
    .PSCLK               (),
    .PSEN                (),
    .PSINCDEC            (),
    .PSDONE              (),
    // Other control and status signals
    .LOCKED              (locked),
    .CLKINSTOPPED        (),
    .CLKFBSTOPPED        (),
    .PWRDWN              (),
    .RST                 (RESET));

  // Output buffering
  //-----------------------------------
  BUFG clkf_buf
   (.O (clkfbout_buf),
    .I (clkfbout));

  BUFG clkout1_buf
   (.O   (CLK_OUT1),
    .I   (clkout0));

  BUFG clkout2_buf
   (.O   (CLK_OUT2),
    .I   (clkout1));

  BUFG clkout3_buf
   (.O   (CLK_OUT3),
    .I   (clkout2));

  assign LOCKED = locked;

endmodule

A Schmitt trigger is a type of digital circuit that converts a noisy input signal into a clean digital signal by using hysteresis. 
The inputs to the circuit are connected to a comparator with two threshold voltages: a high threshold voltage (Vth_high) and a low threshold voltage (Vth_low). 
When the input signal rises above Vth_high, the output of the circuit goes high. 
When the input signal falls below Vth_low, the output of the circuit goes low. 
However, when the input signal is between Vth_high and Vth_low, the output of the circuit holds its previous state.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- in: the input signal
- Vth_high: the high threshold voltage
- Vth_low: the low threshold voltage

Outputs: 
- out: the output signal

Your module should implement the following functionality:
- When the input signal rises above Vth_high, the output signal should go high
- When the input signal falls below Vth_low, the output signal should go low
- When the input signal is between Vth_high and Vth_low, the output signal should hold its previous state

To implement the Schmitt trigger, you should use Verilog code to compare the input signal with the high and low threshold voltages. 
You should then use a flip-flop to store the previous state of the output signal. 
Finally, you should use conditional statements to determine the current state of the output signal based on the input signal and the previous state.

module schmitt_trigger(
  input in,
  input Vth_high,
  input Vth_low,
  output out
);

  reg out_reg; // register to store previous state of output signal

  always @(in, Vth_high, Vth_low, out_reg) begin
    if (in > Vth_high) begin
      out_reg <= 1'b1; // set output to high
    end else if (in < Vth_low) begin
      out_reg <= 1'b0; // set output to low
    end else begin
      out_reg <= out_reg; // hold previous state
    end
  end

  assign out = out_reg; // assign output to stored value

endmodule

The system should include an additional functional module that takes in the outputs of both modules and adds them together to produce a final 4-bit output. The barrel shifter should have a synchronous reset input that sets the output to 0 when high, and the adder-subtractor should have a synchronous reset input that sets the output to 0x0 when high. module top_module (
    input [3:0] DATA,
    input signed [3:0] SHIFT,
    input SUB,
    input RESET,
    input clk,
    output reg [3:0] OUT
);

reg [3:0] shifted_data;
reg [3:0] add_sub_out;

barrel_shifter barrel_shifter_inst (
    .DATA(DATA),
    .SHIFT(SHIFT),
    .OUT(shifted_data),
    .RESET(RESET),
    .clk(clk)
);

adder_subtractor add_sub_inst (
    .A(shifted_data),
    .B(DATA),
    .SUB(SUB),
    .OUT(add_sub_out),
    .RESET(RESET),
    .clk(clk)
);

always @ (posedge clk) begin
    if (RESET) begin
        OUT <= 4'b0000;
    end else begin
        if (SUB) begin
            OUT <= add_sub_out;
        end else begin
            OUT <= add_sub_out + shifted_data;
        end
    end
end

endmodule

module barrel_shifter (
    input [3:0] DATA,
    input signed [3:0] SHIFT,
    output reg [3:0] OUT,
    input RESET,
    input clk
);

always @ (posedge clk) begin
    if (RESET) begin
        OUT <= 4'b0000;
    end else begin
        OUT <= DATA << SHIFT;
    end
end

endmodule

module adder_subtractor (
    input [3:0] A,
    input [3:0] B,

module Counter (

    input reset,
    input count_en,
    input [31:0] max_count,
    output reg [31:0] count
);

            if (count == max_count) begin

);

module AGC (
  input in,
  input ctrl,
  output out
);

parameter k = 10; // gain of amplifier at maximum control signal value
parameter max_val = 100; // maximum output signal amplitude

always @(*) begin

- rst: a reset signal that clears the accumulated sum to zero
- data_in: a signal that receives the sequence of numbers to be accumulated

- max_value: the maximum value that can be accumulated without overflow

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- On the rising edge of the clock signal, the module should add the value of data_in to the accumulated sum.
- If the accumulated sum exceeds the maximum value, the circuit should saturate and not increase further.
- If the reset signal is high, the accumulated sum should be cleared to zero.

To implement the accumulator, you should use Verilog code to define the logic for adding the input values to the accumulated sum and checking for overflow. 
You should also use code to implement the reset functionality. 
Finally, you should use the output signal to provide the accumulated sum.

module accumulator (
  input clk,
  input rst,
  input [n-1:0] data_in,
  output reg [n-1:0] acc_out
);

parameter n = 8; // number of bits in the accumulator
parameter max_value = 255; // maximum value that can be accumulated without overflow

reg [n-1:0] sum; // register to store the accumulated sum

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) begin
    sum <= 0; // clear the accumulated sum to zero
  end else begin
    sum <= (sum + data_in) > max_value ? max_value : (sum + data_in); // add the input value to the accumulated sum and check for overflow
  end
end

assign acc_out = sum; // provide the accumulated sum as output

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a power-on reset generator. 
A power-on reset generator is a digital circuit that generates a reset signal when the power is turned on. 
The reset signal is used to initialize the system to a known state.
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a power supply voltage (Vdd) and a ground voltage (GND)

The module should also have the following parameters:

t_reset: the duration of the reset pulse
t_delay: the delay before the reset pulse is generated
Your module should implement the following functionality:

When the power supply voltage is first applied, the reset signal should be low.
After a delay of t_delay, the reset signal should go high for a duration of t_reset.
After the reset pulse, the reset signal should go low again.

You should use a combination of delay blocks and logical gates to generate the reset signal.

module POR (
  input Vdd,
  input GND,
  output reg reset
);

parameter t_reset = 10; // duration of reset pulse (in ns)
parameter t_delay = 100; // delay before reset pulse (in ns)

reg [1:0] state; // state machine to generate reset signal

always @(posedge Vdd or negedge GND) begin
  if (!GND) begin
    state <= 2'b00; // reset state machine on power-off
    reset <= 1'b0; // reset signal is low on power-off
  end else if (Vdd) begin
    case (state)
      2'b00: begin // wait for delay
        if ($time >= t_delay) begin
          state <= 2'b01; // transition to pulse state
          reset <= 1'b1; // generate reset pulse
        end
      end
      2'b01: begin // generate pulse
        if ($time >= t_delay + t_reset) begin
          state <= 2'b10; // transition to idle state
          reset <= 1'b0; // reset signal goes low
        end
      end
      2'b10: begin // idle state
        // do nothing
      end
    endcase
  end
end

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) memory block. 
A LIFO is a type of memory that stores a set of data elements and retrieves them in the reverse order of their storage. 
Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: 
- input_data: the data to be written to the memory block
- write_en: a write enable signal that indicates when to write input_data to the memory block
- read_en: a read enable signal that indicates when to read data from the memory block

Outputs: 
- output_data: the data read from the memory block

Your module should also have the following parameters:

- depth: the number of data elements that can be stored in the memory block

Your module should implement the following functionality:

- When write_en is high, input_data should be written to the memory block.
- When read_en is high, the most recently written data element should be read from the memory block and output on output_data.
- When the memory block is empty, output_data should remain unchanged.
- When the memory block is full and a new data element is written, the oldest element should be discarded.
- When both write_en and read_en are high, the memory block should write input_data and read the most recently written data element.

To implement the LIFO memory block, you should use Verilog code to define the memory block as an array of depth elements. 
You should then use the write_en and read_en signals to control the writing and reading of data to and from the array. 
Finally, you should use the output_data signal to output the data read from the memory block.

module lifo_memory (
  input [depth-1:0] input_data,
  input write_en,
  input read_en,
  output [depth-1:0] output_data
);

parameter depth = 16; // number of data elements that can be stored in the memory block

reg [depth-1:0] memory [0:depth-1]; // define memory block as an array of depth elements
reg [depth-1:0] read_pointer = depth-1; // initialize read pointer to the last element
reg [depth-1:0] write_pointer = depth-1; // initialize write pointer to the last element

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (write_en) begin
    memory[write_pointer] <= input_data; // write input_data to memory block
    write_pointer <= write_pointer - 1; // decrement write pointer
    if (write_pointer < 0) begin
      write_pointer <= depth-1; // wrap around write pointer if it goes below 0
    end
  end
  if (read_en) begin
    output_data <= memory[read_pointer]; // read data from memory block
    read_pointer <= read_pointer - 1; // decrement read pointer
    if (read_pointer < 0) begin
      read_pointer <= depth-1; // wrap around read pointer if it goes below 0
    end
  end
end

endmodule

module clock_gate (
  input CLK, EN, TE,
  input [31:0] W,
  output reg ENCLK,
  output reg [31:0] Y
);

  always @ (posedge CLK) begin
    if (TE) begin
      ENCLK <= CLK;
    end else begin
      ENCLK <= EN ? CLK : 1'b0;
    end
  end

  always @ (posedge ENCLK) begin
    Y <= W;
  end

endmodule

module shift_mux (
    input clk,
    input areset,
    input load,
    input ena,
    input [3:0] data_in,
    input [2:0] select,
    output reg [3:0] q_shift,
    output reg w, x, y, z,
    output reg [3:0] final_output
);

// Instantiate the 4-bit barrel shifter module
barrel_shifter bs (
    .clk(clk),
    .areset(areset),
    .load(load),
    .ena(ena),
    .data_in(data_in),
    .shift_amount(select),
    .data_out(q_shift)
);

// Instantiate the 3-to-4 multiplexer module
mux3to4 mux (
    .a(q_shift),
    .b(data_in),
    .c({q_shift[2:0], data_in[3]}),
    .select(select),
    .w(w),
    .x(x),
    .y(y),
    .z(z)
);

// Final output is the bitwise OR of the shift register output and the MUX output
assign final_output = q_shift | {w, x, y, z};

endmodule

    input clk,
    input areset,
    input load,
    input ena,
    input [3:0] data_in,
    input [1:0] shift_amount,
    output reg [3:0] data_out
);

always @(posedge clk or posedge areset) begin
    if (areset) begin
        data_out <= 4'b0;
    end else if (load) begin
        data_out <= data_in;
    end else if (ena) begin
        case (shift_amount)
            2'b00: data_out <= data_in;
            2'b01: data_out <= {data_in[0], data_in[3:1]};
            2'b10: data_out <= {data_in[1:0], data_in[3:2]};
            2'b11: data_out <= {data_in[2:0], data_in[3]};
        endcase
    end
end

endmodule

// 3-to-4 multiplexer module
module mux3to4 (
    input [3:0] a,
    input [3:0] b,
    input [3:0] c,
    input [1:0] select,
    output reg w,
    output reg x,
    output reg y,
    output reg z
);

always @* begin
    case (select)
        2'b00: begin w = a; x = b; y = c; z = 4'b0; end
        2'b01: begin w = c; x = a; y = b; z = 4'b0; end
        2'b10: begin w = b; x = c; y = a; z = 4'b0; end
        2'b11: begin w = 4'b0; x = 4'b0; y = 4'b0; z = 4'b1; end
    endcase
end

endmodule

- output [7:0] C: the output register C
- output VALID: goes high for one clock cycle when a calculation is complete

Assume that the inputs A and B are valid on the rising edge of the clock and remain stable until the next rising edge of the clock. Also assume that CTRL is valid on the rising edge of the clock and remains stable until the next rising edge of the clock.

module calculator(
    input clk,
    input rst,
    input [7:0] A,
    input [7:0] B,
    input [1:0] CTRL,
    output [7:0] C,
    output VALID
);

    reg [7:0] C_reg; // Output register
    reg VALID_reg; // Valid signal register

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (rst) begin
            C_reg <= 8'h00;
            VALID_reg <= 1'b0;
        end else begin
            case (CTRL)
                2'b00: C_reg <= A + B; // addition
                2'b01: C_reg <= A - B; // subtraction
                2'b10: C_reg <= A * B; // multiplication
                2'b11: C_reg <= A / B; // division
            endcase

            VALID_reg <= 1'b1; // Set valid signal
        end
    end

    assign C = C_reg;
    assign VALID = VALID_reg;

endmodule

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Your task is to create a Verilog module that implements a glitch filter. A glitch is a momentary disturbance in a digital signal, which can cause errors in digital circuits. A glitch filter is a circuit that removes glitches from a digital signal.

Your glitch filter module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs: a digital signal (signal_in)
Outputs: a filtered digital signal (signal_out)

Your module should implement the following functionality:

The circuit should detect glitches in the input signal.
If a glitch is detected, the circuit should delay the input signal for a certain number of clock cycles.
The circuit should then output the delayed signal as the filtered signal.
If no glitch is detected, the circuit should output the input signal as the filtered signal.

To implement the glitch filter, you should use Verilog code to detect glitches in the input signal. You can do this by comparing the input signal to a delayed version of itself. If the difference between the input signal and the delayed signal is above a certain threshold, a glitch is detected. If a glitch is detected, you should delay the input signal for a certain number of clock cycles before outputting it as the filtered signal.

Your module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:
signal_in: the input digital signal
clk: the clock signal
rst: the reset signal (active low)

Outputs:
signal_out: the filtered digital signal

To implement the glitch filter, you should define a delay line using Verilog code. The delay line should be a shift register that delays the input signal by a certain number of clock cycles. You should use the delay line to compare the input signal to a delayed version of itself, and to delay the input signal when a glitch is detected.
Response:
module glitch_filter (
  input signal_in,
  input clk,
  input rst,
  output signal_out
);

  parameter DELAY_CYCLES = 5; // Number of clock cycles to delay signal_in
  parameter GLITCH_THRESHOLD = 2; // Threshold for glitch detection

  reg [DELAY_CYCLES-1:0] delay_line; // Delay line for signal_in
  reg glitch_detected; // Flag for glitch detection

  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst) begin
    if (!rst) begin
      delay_line <= 0;
      glitch_detected <= 0;
    end
    else begin
      delay_line <= {signal_in, delay_line[DELAY_CYCLES-1:1]};
      if (glitch_detected) begin
        signal_out <= delay_line[DELAY_CYCLES-1];
      end
      else begin
        signal_out <= signal_in;
      end
      if (signal_in - delay_line[DELAY_CYCLES-1] > GLITCH_THRESHOLD || delay_line[DELAY_CYCLES-1] - signal_in > GLITCH_THRESHOLD) begin
        glitch_detected <= 1;
      end
      else if (glitch_detected && delay_line[DELAY_CYCLES-1] == signal_in) begin
        glitch_detected <= 0;
      end
    end
  end

endmodule

);

Please act as a professional Verilog designer. Design a system that incorporates a 100-bit rotator and a 32-bit comparator. The rotator should be able to rotate the bits around without modifying or discarding them. The system should also include a 4-bit input port for selecting the direction of rotation and a 1-bit input port for loading data into the rotator. The output port of the rotator should be connected to a 128-bit shift register, which should shift the output by one bit on every rising edge of the clock. The comparator should capture the transition of the 32-bit input vector from 0 to 1 using an asynchronous reset and generate an output vector that remains high until the next rising edge of the clock. The functional module should perform a bitwise OR operation on the two inputs to produce the 132-bit output.

module rotator (
    input [99:0] data,
    input [3:0] dir,
    input load,
    output reg [99:0] out
);

always @(*) begin
    case (dir)
        4'b0000: out = data; // no rotation
        4'b0001: out = {data[98:0], data[99]}; // rotate left by 1 bit
        4'b0010: out = {data[97:0], data[99:98]}; // rotate left by 2 bits
        4'b0011: out = {data[96:0], data[99:97]}; // rotate left by 3 bits
        4'b0100: out = {data[95:0], data[99:96]}; // rotate left by 4 bits
        4'b0101: out = {data[94:0], data[99:95]}; // rotate left by 5 bits
        4'b0110: out = {data[93:0], data[99:94]}; // rotate left by 6 bits
        4'b0111: out = {data[92:0], data[99:93]}; // rotate left by 7 bits
        4'b1000: out = {data[1:0], data[99:2]}; // rotate right by 1 bit
        4'b1001: out = {data[2:0], data[99:3]}; // rotate right by 2 bits
        4'b1010: out = {data[3:0], data[99:4]}; // rotate right by 3 bits
        4'b1011: out = {data[4:0], data[99:5]}; // rotate right by 4 bits
        4'b1100: out = {data[5:0], data[99:6]}; // rotate right by 5 bits
        4'b1101: out = {data[6:0], data[99:7]}; // rotate right by 6 bits
        4'b1110: out = {data[7:0], data[99:8]}; // rotate right by 7 bits
        4'b1111: out = data; // no rotation
    endcase
end

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) begin
        out <= 0;
    end else if (load) begin
        out <= data;
    end else begin
        out <= {out[98:0], out[99]};
    end
end

endmodule

module comparator (
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input [31:0] in,
    output reg out
);

always @(posedge clk or negedge reset) begin
    if (reset == 0) begin
        out <= 0;
    end else if (in == 32'h00000001) begin
        out <= 1;
    end
end

endmodule

module functional_module (
    input [131:0] in1,
    input [131:0] in2,
    output [131:0] out
);

assign out = in1 | in2;

endmodule

module top_module (
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input load,
    input [3:0] dir,
    input [99:0] data,
    input [31:0] in,
    output [131:0] out
);

wire [99:0] rotator_out;
wire [127:0] shift_register_out;
wire comparator_out;

rotator rotator_inst (
    .data(data),
    .dir(dir),
    .load(load),
    .out(rotator_out)
);

shift_register shift_register_inst (
    .clk(clk),
    .reset(reset),
    .in(rotator_out),
    .out(shift_register_out)
);

comparator comparator_inst (
    .clk(clk),
    .reset(reset),
    .in(in),
    .out(comparator_out)
);

functional_module functional_module_inst (
    .in1(shift_register_out),
    .in2({132{comparator_out}}),
    .out(out)
);

endmodule

    input en_ff,

);

    input CLK,
    input RESET,
    input LOAD,
    input [3:0] LOAD_VAL,
    output reg [3:0] Q
);

        if (RESET) begin
            Q <= 4'b0;
        end else if (LOAD) begin
            Q <= LOAD_VAL;
        end else begin
            Q <= Q + 1;
        end

endmodule

   input clk,
   input rst,
   input inc,
   input dec,
   output reg [3:0] cnt
);

      end
      else if (inc && !dec) begin

            cnt <= 0;
         end
         else begin

         end

endmodule

module wb_stream_writer
  #(parameter WB_DW = 32,
    parameter WB_AW = 32,
    parameter FIFO_AW = 0,
    parameter MAX_BURST_LEN = 2**FIFO_AW)
   (input         clk,
    input                rst,
    //Wishbone memory interface
    output [WB_AW-1:0]   wbm_adr_o,
    output [WB_DW-1:0]   wbm_dat_o,
    output [WB_DW/8-1:0] wbm_sel_o,
    output               wbm_we_o ,
    output               wbm_cyc_o,
    output               wbm_stb_o,
    output [2:0]         wbm_cti_o,
    output [1:0]         wbm_bte_o,
    input [WB_DW-1:0]    wbm_dat_i,
    input                wbm_ack_i,
    input                wbm_err_i,
    //Stream interface
    output [WB_DW-1:0]   stream_m_data_o,
    output               stream_m_valid_o,
    input                stream_m_ready_i,
    output               stream_m_irq_o,
    //Configuration interface
    input [4:0]          wbs_adr_i,
    input [WB_DW-1:0]    wbs_dat_i,
    input [WB_DW/8-1:0]  wbs_sel_i,
    input                wbs_we_i ,
    input                wbs_cyc_i,
    input                wbs_stb_i,
    input [2:0]          wbs_cti_i,
    input [1:0]          wbs_bte_i,
    output [WB_DW-1:0]   wbs_dat_o,
    output               wbs_ack_o,
    output               wbs_err_o);

   //FIFO interface
   wire [WB_DW-1:0]     fifo_din;
   wire [FIFO_AW:0]     fifo_cnt;
   wire         fifo_rd;
   wire         fifo_wr;

   //Configuration parameters
   wire         enable;
   wire [WB_DW-1:0]     tx_cnt;
   wire [WB_AW-1:0]     start_adr; 
   wire [WB_AW-1:0]     buf_size;
   wire [WB_AW-1:0]     burst_size;

   wire         busy;
   
   wb_stream_writer_ctrl
     #(.WB_AW (WB_AW),
       .WB_DW (WB_DW),
       .FIFO_AW (FIFO_AW),
       .MAX_BURST_LEN (MAX_BURST_LEN))
   ctrl
     (.wb_clk_i    (clk),
      .wb_rst_i    (rst),
      //Stream data output
      .wbm_adr_o (wbm_adr_o),
      .wbm_dat_o (wbm_dat_o),
      .wbm_sel_o (wbm_sel_o),
      .wbm_we_o  (wbm_we_o),
      .wbm_cyc_o (wbm_cyc_o),
      .wbm_stb_o (wbm_stb_o),
      .wbm_cti_o (wbm_cti_o),
      .wbm_bte_o (wbm_bte_o),
      .wbm_dat_i (wbm_dat_i),
      .wbm_ack_i (wbm_ack_i),
      .wbm_err_i (wbm_err_i),
      //FIFO interface
      .fifo_d    (fifo_din),
      .fifo_wr   (fifo_wr),
      .fifo_cnt  (fifo_cnt),
      //Configuration interface
      .busy       (busy),
      .enable     (enable),
      .tx_cnt     (tx_cnt),
      .start_adr  (start_adr),
      .buf_size   (buf_size),
      .burst_size (burst_size));

   wb_stream_writer_cfg
     #(.WB_AW (WB_AW),
       .WB_DW (WB_DW))
   cfg
     (.wb_clk_i  (clk),
      .wb_rst_i  (rst),
      //Wishbone IF
      .wb_adr_i (wbs_adr_i),
      .wb_dat_i (wbs_dat_i),
      .wb_sel_i (wbs_sel_i),
      .wb_we_i  (wbs_we_i),
      .wb_cyc_i (wbs_cyc_i),
      .wb_stb_i (wbs_stb_i),
      .wb_cti_i (wbs_cti_i),
      .wb_bte_i (wbs_bte_i),
      .wb_dat_o (wbs_dat_o),
      .wb_ack_o (wbs_ack_o),
      .wb_err_o (wbs_err_o),
      //Application IF
      .irq       (stream_m_irq_o),
      .busy      (busy),
      .enable    (enable),
      .tx_cnt    (tx_cnt),
      .start_adr (start_adr),
      .buf_size  (buf_size),
      .burst_size (burst_size));

   wb_stream_writer_fifo
     #(.DW (WB_DW),
       .AW (FIFO_AW))
   fifo0
   (.clk   (clk),
    .rst   (rst),

    .stream_s_data_i  (fifo_din),
    .stream_s_valid_i (fifo_wr),
    .stream_s_ready_o (),

    .stream_m_data_o  (stream_m_data_o),
    .stream_m_valid_o (stream_m_valid_o),
    .stream_m_ready_i (stream_m_ready_i),

    .cnt   (fifo_cnt));

endmodule

When sel_b1 and sel_b2 are both high, the output should be the BCD value. Otherwise, the output should be the 8-bit input value. The final output should be a 16-bit binary-coded decimal value.

module bcd_counter_mux(
    input clk,
    input reset,       // Synchronous active-high reset
    input [7:0] in,    // 8-bit input signal for the multiplexer
    output [3:1] ena,  // Enable signals for the BCD counter
    input sel_b1,      // Selection signal for the multiplexer
    input sel_b2,      // Selection signal for the multiplexer
    output reg [15:0] q // 16-bit binary-coded decimal output signal
);

reg [3:0] count;        // 4-bit binary counter
reg [3:0] bcd;          // 4-bit BCD counter
wire [6:0] bcd_enc;     // 7-bit BCD encoder output
wire [3:0] sel;         // 4-bit selection signal for the BCD counter

// BCD encoder
bcd_encoder bcd_enc_inst(
    .in(count),
    .out(bcd_enc)
);

// BCD counter
bcd_counter bcd_counter_inst(
    .clk(clk),
    .reset(reset),
    .bcd_in(bcd_enc),
    .sel(sel),
    .ena(ena)
);

// Multiplexer
always @ (sel_b1, sel_b2, bcd, in) begin
    if (sel_b1 && sel_b2) begin
        q = {bcd, 4'b0000};
    end else begin
        q = {in, 8'b00000000};
    end
end

// Selection signal for the BCD counter
always @ (count) begin
    case (count)
        4'b0000: sel = 4'b1000; // Enable only the fourth digit
        4'b0001: sel = 4'b0100; // Enable only the third digit
        4'b0010: sel = 4'b0010; // Enable only the second digit
        4'b0011: sel = 4'b0001; // Enable only the first digit
        default: sel = 4'b0000; // Disable all digits
    endcase
end

// Binary counter
always @ (posedge clk, posedge reset) begin
    if (reset) begin
        count <= 4'b0000;
    end else begin
        count <= count + 1;
    end
end

endmodule

);

Write a Verilog module that implements this memory design. The module should have the following inputs and outputs:

Inputs:

- mem_rd_en: A read enable signal for the memory module.
- mem_rd_addr: A 2-bit address input for the memory module.
- bist_clk: The clock signal used for the BIST feature.
- bist_en: A signal that enables the BIST feature.
- bist_addr: A 2-bit address input for the BIST feature.
- bist_wr_data: A 64-bit data input for the BIST feature.

- mem_rd_data: A 64-bit data output for the memory module.
- bist_rd_data: A 64-bit data output for the BIST feature.

module mem_16nm_ram4x64
(
  input  wire        clk,
  input  wire        mem_wr_en,
  input  wire [1:0]  mem_wr_addr,
  input  wire [63:0] mem_wr_data,
  input  wire        mem_rd_en,
  input  wire [1:0]  mem_rd_addr,
  output wire [63:0] mem_rd_data,

  input  wire        bist_clk,
  input  wire        bist_en,
  input  wire [1:0]  bist_addr,
  input  wire [63:0] bist_wr_data,
  output wire [63:0] bist_rd_data
);

// The memory declaration
reg [63:0] memory [3:0];
reg [63:0] mem_rd_data_i;

always @ (posedge clk) begin
  if( mem_wr_en ) begin
    memory[mem_wr_addr] <= #0 mem_wr_data;
  end

  if( mem_rd_en ) begin
    mem_rd_data_i <= #0 memory[mem_rd_addr];
  end
end

always @ (posedge clk) begin
  mem_rd_data <= #0 mem_rd_data_i;
end

// Bist fake logic
always @ (posedge bist_clk ) begin
  if( bist_en ) begin
    bist_rd_data <= #0 memory[bist_addr];
    memory[bist_addr] <= #0 bist_wr_data;
  end
end

endmodule

module gray_to_binary (
    input G2,
    input G1,
    input G0,
    output reg B2,
    output reg B1,
    output reg B0
);

always @ (G2, G1, G0) begin
    case ({G2, G1, G0})
        3'b000: begin B2 = 1'b0; B1 = 1'b0; B0 = 1'b0; end
        3'b001: begin B2 = 1'b0; B1 = 1'b0; B0 = 1'b1; end
        3'b010: begin B2 = 1'b0; B1 = 1'b1; B0 = 1'b1; end
        3'b011: begin B2 = 1'b0; B1 = 1'b1; B0 = 1'b0; end

        3'b110: begin B2 = 1'b1; B1 = 1'b0; B0 = 1'b1; end
        3'b111: begin B2 = 1'b1; B1 = 1'b0; B0 = 1'b0; end
    endcase
end

endmodule

module shift_register (
    input [7:0] data_in,
    input shift,
    input load,
    output reg [7:0] data_out
);

always @ (posedge shift or posedge load) begin
    if (load) begin
        data_out <= data_in;
    end else if (shift) begin
        data_out <= {data_out[6:0], data_out[7]};
    end
end

endmodule

module bitwise_and (
    input [2:0] binary_in,
    input [7:0] shift_in,
    output reg [7:0] out
);

always @ (binary_in, shift_in) begin
    out = binary_in & shift_in;
end

endmodule

);

endmodule

    input wire Reset,
    input wire Up_Down,
    input wire Enable,

);

    - `max_val_p`: maximum value that the counter can reach
    - `init_val_p`: initial value of the counter (default value is 0)
    - `ptr_width_lp`: width of the `count_o` output
    - `disable_overflow_warning_p`: flag to disable overflow warning (default value is 0)
- The module should handle overflow and underflow conditions.

Response:
module up_clear_counter #(parameter max_val_p = 255,
                          parameter init_val_p = 0,
                          parameter ptr_width_lp = 8,
                          parameter disable_overflow_warning_p = 0)
    (input clk_i, reset_i, clear_i, up_i,
     output reg [ptr_width_lp-1:0] count_o);

    always @(posedge clk_i) begin
        if (reset_i) begin
            count_o <= init_val_p;
        end else begin
            if (clear_i) begin
                count_o <= 0;
            end else begin
                if (up_i) begin
                    if (count_o == max_val_p) begin
                        if (!disable_overflow_warning_p) begin
                            $display("%m error: counter overflow at time %t", $time);
                        end
                    end else begin
                        count_o <= count_o + 1;
                    end
                end else begin
                    if (count_o == 0) begin
                        count_o <= max_val_p;
                    end else begin
                        count_o <= count_o - 1;
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end

endmodule

An Adler checksum is a type of cyclic redundancy check (CRC) that is used to detect errors in data transmission. 
The checksum is calculated by computing two 16-bit sums of the data, which are then combined to form a 32-bit checksum.
